With a thankful. heart to the British people for the life of Charles. Spurgeon.  Praying for your nation to recover as well as ours.

This day is notable in English history for two great deliverances wrought by God for us. On this day the plot of the Papists to destroy our Houses of Parliament was discovered, 1605.

   "While for our princes they prepare
   In caverns deep a burning snare,
   He shot from heaven a piercing ray,
   And the dark treachery brought to day."
And secondly-to-day is the anniversary of the landing of King William III, at Torbay, by which the hope of Popish ascendancy was quashed, and religious liberty was secured, 1688.
This day ought to be celebrated, not by the saturnalia of striplings, but by the songs of saints. Our Puritan forefathers most devoutly made it a special time of thanksgiving. There is extant a record of the annual sermons preached by Matthew Henry on this day. Our Protestant feeling, and our love of liberty, should make us regard its anniversary with holy gratitude. Let our hearts and lips exclaim, "We have heard with our ears, and our fathers have told us the wondrous things which thou didst in their day, and in the old time before them." Thou hast made this nation the home of the gospel; and when the foe has risen against her, thou hast shielded her. Help us to offer repeated songs for repeated deliverances. Grant us more and more a hatred of Antichrist, and hasten on the day of her entire extinction. Till then and ever, we believe the promise, "No weapon that is formed against thee shall prosper." Should it not be laid upon the heart of every lover of the gospel of Jesus on this day to plead for the overturning of false doctrines and the extension of divine truth? Would it not be well to search our own hearts, and turn out any of the Popish lumber of self-righteousness which may lie concealed therein?

text:
$PLTK Q3 2026 earnings: Playtika's profit hits a record, but its player base shrinks

Playtika, the maker of mobile games such as Bingo Blitz, lifted its profit by cutting marketing even as its player base shrank. Third-quarter revenue held steady at $674 million while operating cash profit rose 16% to a record $252 million, and the board ended its seven-month strategic review to stay independent. Finance chief Tae Lee raised the full-year target from the bottom of the range back to the middle, though by our math that plan still has fourth-quarter sales falling 4%.

• Revenue: $𝟔𝟕𝟑.𝟖𝐌 (-0.1% from a year ago)
• Operating cash profit (Adjusted EBITDA): $𝟐𝟓𝟐.𝟏𝐌 (+15.9% from a year ago (37.4% margin))
• Daily active users: 𝟕.𝟏𝐌 (-13.4% from a year ago)
• Full-year outlook: 𝐑𝐚𝐢𝐬𝐞𝐝 𝐭𝐨 𝐦𝐢𝐝𝐝𝐥𝐞 ($2.80B revenue and $770M Adjusted EBITDA)

⚖️ 𝐕𝐞𝐫𝐝𝐢𝐜𝐭: ⚪ Neutral

The story is unchanged because higher profit margins from planned marketing cuts balanced out deeper player losses across older games. Pulling back on advertising rebuilt the cash pile to $595 million and lifted direct payments past 40% of sales, easing immediate cash pressure ahead of the 2027 debt deadlines. The bad news: daily players dropped 13%, Bingo Blitz sales fell 18%, and Disney Solitaire's growth added another $80 million to the acquisition payout bill.

The question now is whether Disney Solitaire can keep its players without heavy advertising while Playtika refinances its 2027 and 2028 debt. Either the card game holds its audience and generates cash to pay down debt, or its sales keep sliding alongside Bingo Blitz while earnout bills drain the cash pile. Fourth-quarter revenue for Disney Solitaire and a refinancing update before March 2027 will tell.

Full article with charts - link in bio

🐂 𝐁𝐮𝐥𝐥 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🟢🟢 𝐏𝐥𝐚𝐧𝐧𝐞𝐝 𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐤𝐞𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐂𝐮𝐭 𝐃𝐫𝐨𝐯𝐞 𝐑𝐞𝐜𝐨𝐫𝐝 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐟𝐢𝐭 𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐢𝐧
Playtika spent heavily on player marketing in the first half of the year and promised to pull back in the second half. Finance chief Tae Lee said "marketing stepped down as planned, Adjusted EBITDA margin expanded to 37.4%, and we delivered record quarterly Adjusted EBITDA of $252.1 million".

Advertising and overhead fell to 24.9% of sales, down 5.7 percentage points from a year ago and 9.7 percentage points from last quarter. Game development costs also dropped 1.8 percentage points of sales to 12.9% after January's staff cuts. That cost discipline lifted operating cash profit 15.9% from a year ago even though revenue barely moved, allowing Playtika to raise its full-year target back to the middle of its range.

What to watch: fourth-quarter advertising and overhead spending. By our math, the full-year outlook points to an operating cash profit margin of about 28.7% in the fourth quarter, which would mean marketing rises again before year-end.

🟢 𝐃𝐢𝐫𝐞𝐜𝐭 𝐏𝐚𝐲𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐏𝐥𝐚𝐭𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐦 𝐏𝐚𝐬𝐬𝐞𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝟒𝟎% 𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐤
Playtika steers players to its own payment platform — Direct-to-Consumer, or DTC — to avoid the 30% commission that Apple and Google charge in their app stores. Management had aimed for direct payments to reach 40% of sales within two years of setting the goal last autumn, after the share stalled at 39.2% for two straight quarters.

Direct-to-Consumer revenue grew 31.4% from a year ago to $275.1 million, reaching 40.8% of total sales by our math and passing the 40% goal a year early. Because direct sales fell 4.1% from last quarter while total sales fell 7.8%, the share gain came from app-store revenue shrinking faster as marketing dropped. That shift still protected gross margin, which rose 0.5 percentage points from a year ago to 74.0%.

What to watch: whether management sets a higher Direct-to-Consumer target at year-end. Without a move past 41%, the yearly fee savings from shifting away from app stores will fade in 2027.

🐻 𝐁𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🔴🔴 𝐏𝐥𝐚𝐲𝐞𝐫 𝐂𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐭𝐬 𝐒𝐡𝐫𝐚𝐧𝐤 𝐀𝐜𝐫𝐨𝐬𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐏𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐟𝐨𝐥𝐢𝐨
"With the strategic review complete, we are moving forward as an independent company. Our third quarter reflects what makes Playtika durable: loyal players and games built to last," chief executive Robert Antokol said. Yet the user numbers show fewer people playing Playtika's games, and its largest older title lost ground faster.

• Daily active users: 7.1 million, down 13.4% from a year ago and 11.3% from last quarter
• Monthly active users: 21.5 million, down 18.6% from a year ago
• Daily paying users: 333,000, down 5.9% from a year ago
• Bingo Blitz revenue: $133.0 million, down 18.2% from a year ago after falling 9.5% in the second quarter
• Sales outside Disney Solitaire: $562.6 million, down 8.6% from a year ago by our math

Playtika kept total revenue steady only because average daily revenue per active user rose 15.7% from a year ago to $1.03, and because payer conversion — the share of daily players who spend money — reached 4.7%. Squeezing more money from a shrinking group of players has limits, and the full-year outlook points to total revenue falling 4.2% from a year ago in the fourth quarter by our math.

What to watch: daily active users and Bingo Blitz sales in the fourth quarter. Another double-digit drop in Bingo Blitz would show that older titles are shrinking faster than new games can replace them.

🔴🔴 𝐒𝐮𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐏𝐥𝐚𝐲 𝐄𝐚𝐫𝐧𝐨𝐮𝐭 𝐋𝐢𝐚𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐢𝐭𝐲 𝐉𝐮𝐦𝐩𝐞𝐝 𝐀𝐧𝐨𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 $𝟖𝟎 𝐌𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧
Playtika bought game studio SuperPlay in late 2024 for $700 million upfront plus up to $1.25 billion in future cash payments — known as contingent consideration or earnouts — tied to revenue growth and profit margins through 2027. SuperPlay's hit card game Disney Solitaire is the company's main growth engine, but every jump in its performance increases the cash bill owed to SuperPlay's sellers.

Disney Solitaire revenue rose 88.4% from a year ago to $111.2 million, though it dropped 21.9% from last quarter when marketing stepped down. That performance forced Playtika to record an $80.0 million charge in general and administrative expenses for the rising value of the earnout, bringing the nine-month charge to $177.0 million. After paying $350.0 million of earnouts in financing cash flow this year, Playtika still carries $450.0 million of earnout liabilities on its balance sheet, including $320.0 million due within a year.

What to watch: the exact second-year SuperPlay earnout bill at year-end, payable in the second quarter of 2027. A payment near the $320.0 million current liability would consume more than half of Playtika's current cash.

🔴 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐑𝐞𝐛𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐝𝐞𝐝 𝐁𝐞𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐃𝐞𝐛𝐭 𝐑𝐞𝐟𝐢𝐧𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐃𝐞𝐚𝐝𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐞𝐬
Playtika faces a $550 million credit line expiring in March 2027 and a $1.8 billion term loan maturing in March 2028, after its Chinese-owned controlling shareholder's regulatory status previously blocked a longer credit-line extension. To preserve cash for debt and earnouts, management suspended the quarterly dividend at the start of 2026 and bought back no shares this year.

Cash and short-term investments rebounded to $594.6 million from $438.7 million in June, helped by $162.5 million of third-quarter free cash flow by our math. Lee said Playtika intends to build on its discipline by "strengthening our balance sheet". Still, total debt stands at $2.38 billion — leaving $1.79 billion of net debt by our math — and the company has not yet refinanced either facility.

What to watch: an announcement on the $550 million credit line before it expires in March 2027. A renewal or paydown without Chinese regulatory hurdles would show that the controlling shareholder's status does not block refinancing the 2028 term loan.

🔴 𝐑𝐢𝐬𝐤𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐪𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐝𝐢𝐝𝐧'𝐭 𝐚𝐧𝐬𝐰𝐞𝐫
Three standing legal, tax and operational risks received no update in the third-quarter earnings release.

• Social-casino gambling lawsuits: no mention of the Washington State Attorney General suit, mass arbitrations or state class actions; the quarterly filing's legal footnote will carry the reading.
• Israeli tax assessments: no update on the roughly $159 million of disputed 2017–2021 tax orders; the quarterly filing's tax note will show any settlement or provision.
• Operations in Israel and Ukraine: listed only in standard risk boilerplate; the quarterly filing will show whether the conflicts disrupted studios or raised costs.

👓 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐓𝐡𝐞𝐦𝐞𝐬

𝐁𝐨𝐚𝐫𝐝 𝐄𝐧𝐝𝐞𝐝 𝐒𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐠𝐢𝐜 𝐑𝐞𝐯𝐢𝐞𝐰 𝐖𝐢𝐭𝐡 𝐍𝐨 𝐃𝐞𝐚𝐥
Seven months after launching a review of strategic alternatives in April 2026, Playtika's board ended the process without a sale or transaction. The board decided that Playtika will "continue to operate as an independent, publicly traded company", removing both the chance of a buyout and the uncertainty around a deal shaped by its controlling shareholder.

— • — • —

💲 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐊𝐏𝐈𝐬

𝐍𝐞𝐭 𝐢𝐧𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐞, 𝐞𝐱𝐜𝐥𝐮𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐨𝐧𝐞-𝐨𝐟𝐟𝐬 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟏𝟐𝟎.𝟕 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
Profit excluding one-offs — which strips out the $80.0 million SuperPlay earnout charge and $4.1 million of impairments — rose 83.4% from a year ago and more than doubled from $53.6 million in the second quarter. GAAP net income rose 3.3% to $40.4 million because the earnout charge and a $52.0 million tax bill offset the lower marketing spend.

𝐉𝐮𝐧𝐞'𝐬 𝐉𝐨𝐮𝐫𝐧𝐞𝐲 𝐫𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟕𝟔.𝟔 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
Playtika's nine-year-old hidden-object game grew 12.1% from a year ago and 2.4% from last quarter. That marks its third straight quarter of yearly growth — up from 8.1% in the second quarter and 10.4% in the first — making it the only disclosed older title expanding while Bingo Blitz shrinks.

𝐃𝐢𝐥𝐮𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐬𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐜𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐭 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): 𝟑𝟖𝟐.𝟗 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
The mobile game maker's diluted share count rose 4.0% from a year ago, faster than the 1.8% yearly rise in the second quarter and 0.6% in the first. Playtika spent nothing on share buybacks during the first nine months of 2026 while employee stock awards continued to add shares.

— • — • —

🔮 𝐆𝐮𝐢𝐝𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟔 𝐑𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞: $𝟐.𝟕𝟓–𝟐.𝟖𝟓 𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
🠅 raised from $2.75–2.85 billion (pointed toward the lower end)
Raised within the range. Playtika kept its $2.75–2.85 billion range but now expects to finish "around the midpoint of both ranges" ($2.80 billion, or 1.6% yearly growth) instead of the low end ($2.75 billion). By our math, that midpoint leaves $650.4 million of revenue for the fourth quarter, a 4.2% drop from a year ago. It is the third directional shift this year: raised $50 million in the first quarter, pointed $50 million lower in the second, and lifted $50 million back to the middle today.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟔 𝐀𝐝𝐣𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐄𝐁𝐈𝐓𝐃𝐀: $𝟕𝟓𝟎–𝟕𝟗𝟎 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
🠅 raised from $750–790 million (pointed toward the lower end)
Raised within the range. Management lifted its target from the low end ($750 million) back to the middle of the range ($770 million, or 2.2% growth from a year ago) after the third-quarter marketing pullback. By our math, the $770 million midpoint leaves $186.6 million of Adjusted EBITDA for the fourth quarter — down 7.3% from a year ago and a 28.7% margin against 37.4% in the third quarter. Playtika has met or beaten its full-year Adjusted EBITDA target for two straight years.

— • — • —

❓ 𝐊𝐞𝐲 𝐐𝐮𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬

𝐇𝐨𝐰 𝐦𝐮𝐜𝐡 𝐝𝐢𝐝 𝐬𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬 𝐞𝐱𝐜𝐥𝐮𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐒𝐮𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐏𝐥𝐚𝐲 𝐬𝐡𝐫𝐢𝐧𝐤 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐪𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫?
Disney Solitaire grew 88.4% from a year ago to $111.2 million while total company revenue dipped 0.1%. Management has not disclosed total revenue for the acquired SuperPlay studio, which is needed to see how fast Playtika's older games are declining.

𝐇𝐨𝐰 𝐰𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐏𝐥𝐚𝐲𝐭𝐢𝐤𝐚 𝐡𝐚𝐧𝐝𝐥𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐜𝐡 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟕 𝐜𝐫𝐞𝐝𝐢𝐭 𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐞 𝐞𝐱𝐩𝐢𝐫𝐲?
The $550 million credit facility expires in four months, and the $1.8 billion term loan matures a year later. Investors need to know whether Playtika will let the credit line lapse using its $594.6 million cash pile or extend it without Chinese regulatory blocks.

𝐖𝐡𝐲 𝐝𝐢𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐭𝐚𝐱 𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐣𝐮𝐦𝐩 𝐭𝐨 $𝟓𝟐 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧?
Income tax expense reached $52.0 million on $92.4 million of pre-tax profit — a 56% tax rate — even after a $3.8 million tax benefit on adjustments. The release does not explain whether non-deductible earnout charges or Israeli tax disputes caused the jump.

𝐖𝐡𝐲 𝐝𝐢𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐛𝐨𝐚𝐫𝐝 𝐞𝐧𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐠𝐢𝐜 𝐫𝐞𝐯𝐢𝐞𝐰 𝐰𝐢𝐭𝐡𝐨𝐮𝐭 𝐚 𝐝𝐞𝐚𝐥?
The board concluded its seven-month review of strategic alternatives and chose to stay an independent public company. Shareholders still do not know whether Playtika received buyout offers or whether the controlling shareholder's requirements prevented a sale.

Strong matches
Idaho — Consistently one of the safest states by violent-crime and overall safety metrics (often top 5–10 in recent rankings). Deep red (high R+ partisan index), held Republican in the 2026 midterms, growing but still relatively affordable outside Boise, strong outdoor lifestyle, and lower property crime. Good balance of politics, safety, and livability.​
Thehonestlocal
Wyoming — Among the reddest states in the country and ranks very high on low violent crime (often top 5–6). Extremely low population density, no state income tax, and it stayed firmly Republican. Quiet and conservative, though winters are harsh and services are more spread out.​
@infodexx
Utah — Solidly red, frequently ranks well on broader “safest states” lists (including WalletHub-style measures that factor in crime, roads, and finances), strong economy, family-oriented culture, and relatively low crime. Cost of living is higher than the cheapest red states but still manageable compared with coastal blue areas.
Other solid red + practical notes
States like Alabama, Arkansas, Kentucky, Oklahoma, South Dakota, West Virginia, and North Dakota are reliably red and often among the most affordable (especially housing). They held up well politically in 2026, but crime rates vary more—some score better on pure violent crime (e.g., Kentucky, Wyoming-tier numbers in places) while others rank lower on overall safety metrics.​
Repit

Quick practical filters for you
On a fixed income, prioritize places with lower housing costs (West Virginia, Arkansas, Oklahoma, Alabama, and the Dakotas often lead). Weather, healthcare access, and proximity to family will matter more than the statewide average once you narrow it down.

text:
THE ELECTION IS OVER. THE IRAN WAR ISN’T. NOW WHAT DOES PRESIDENT TRUMP DO?

TRUTHMATTERS NEWS | NOVEMBER 5, 2026
AMERICANS HAVE CHANGED WHO CONTROLS CONGRESS. BUT THE DECISION THAT COULD CHANGE THE IRAN WAR STILL LIES AHEAD.

Following Republican losses in the November 3 midterm elections, President Donald Trump faces renewed pressure over the eight-month conflict with Iran.

According to November 5 reporting by the Associated Press, Trump acknowledged that the war had carried political costs, including higher gasoline prices, but defended his decision to begin military operations.

Vice President JD Vance also identified the war as a significant factor in Republican election losses.

Democrats are projected to control both chambers of Congress when the new Congress convenes January 3, 2027.

But the election did not automatically end the war, authorize new strikes or transfer military command to Congress.

THE POLITICAL CONSEQUENCES ARE VISIBLE. THE NEXT MILITARY DECISION REMAINS UNKNOWN.

WHAT CHOICES DOES THE PRESIDENT FACE?

The conflict began with U.S.-Israeli strikes against Iran on February 28.

The administration now faces several potential courses of action.

CONTINUED MILITARY PRESSURE: Maintain existing operations and demands while attempting to influence Iran’s decisions.

DIPLOMATIC NEGOTIATIONS: Pursue an agreement addressing the underlying security disputes and conditions for reducing hostilities.

MILITARY ESCALATION: Authorize additional attacks if the administration determines its objectives are not being met.

These are possible courses of action, not confirmed new orders.

Trump has previously discussed further military action if Iran rejects terms the United States considers acceptable.

But threatening additional strikes is not the same as ordering or executing them.

ARE FALLING OIL PRICES A SIGN OF PEACE?

Energy markets have reacted sharply to expectations that the election could encourage de-escalation.

AP reported Brent crude falling approximately 8.7% to $94.62 per barrel on November 4.

Lower oil prices may reflect expectations of reduced supply disruptions or changing geopolitical risks.

But financial markets anticipate possibilities. They do not establish future diplomatic outcomes.

A FALLING OIL PRICE IS NOT A PEACE AGREEMENT.

And lower crude prices do not necessarily produce immediate, equivalent reductions in gasoline or household expenses.

DID THE WAR COST REPUBLICANS CONGRESS?

The conflict became an important election issue alongside inflation and household affordability.

Trump and Vance acknowledged its political consequences.

But determining exactly how much the war contributed to individual election outcomes requires more than statements from political leaders.

Voters may have considered economic conditions, candidates, government performance, foreign policy and other concerns simultaneously.

The results demonstrate substantial Republican losses.

They do not prove the war was the sole cause.

WHAT CAN THE NEW CONGRESS ACTUALLY DO?

Congress possesses constitutional authority involving military funding, legislation, oversight and declarations of war.

The president retains substantial commander-in-chief responsibilities.

A Democratic-controlled Congress could pursue investigations, request military information, debate war-powers legislation or seek changes to appropriations.

But the incoming Congress does not assume authority until January.

And congressional control does not automatically compel an immediate military withdrawal.

Legislation may require presidential approval or sufficient votes to override a veto.

The constitutional boundaries of presidential and congressional war powers have also been disputed historically.

KEY PERSPECTIVES

TRUMP ADMINISTRATION: Defends the original military decision while maintaining pressure on Iran. Political statements alone do not independently establish military necessity.

DEMOCRATIC LEADERSHIP: Could pursue greater oversight and changes to war-related spending or policy. The scope of future action remains unknown.

NATIONAL SECURITY CONCERNS: Supporters of continued pressure argue that unresolved security threats may require sustained deterrence. The effectiveness of that approach is not guaranteed.

DIPLOMATIC AND HUMANITARIAN CONCERNS: Advocates of negotiation emphasize the risks and costs of prolonged warfare. A negotiated settlement would still depend on terms acceptable to the parties.

AMERICAN HOUSEHOLDS: Energy-price volatility affects transportation and living costs, although the effects vary.

WHAT WE STILL DON’T KNOW

Will negotiations advance?

What conditions would the United States and Iran accept?

Will additional strikes be ordered?

What are the complete military, civilian and economic costs of the conflict?

How will the new Congress exercise oversight and spending authority?

And what evidence will the administration provide to justify its next decision?

EVIDENCE STATUS

REPORTED: Trump and Vance acknowledged political consequences from the war while Trump continued defending his original decision.

DOCUMENTED: The conflict began in February, Republicans suffered substantial midterm losses, and oil markets reacted to changing expectations.

PARTIALLY ESTABLISHED: The degree to which the war influenced individual voters.

DISPUTED: Whether military pressure or diplomatic concessions offer a more effective path toward resolving the underlying security disputes.

NOT ESTABLISHED: That a comprehensive peace agreement is imminent, new attacks have been ordered or the election legally requires withdrawal.

THE TRUTHMATTERS NEWS TAKEAWAY

ELECTIONS CAN CHANGE POLITICAL PRESSURE. THEY DO NOT AUTOMATICALLY RESOLVE MILITARY CONFLICTS.

President Trump faces consequential decisions involving American forces, regional security, diplomacy and household economic pressures.

The incoming Congress will have opportunities to examine those decisions and exercise its own constitutional powers.

But neither falling oil prices nor election results establish what happens next.

The public deserves to know the administration’s objectives, the evidence supporting continued military action, the costs incurred and the alternatives being considered.

THE QUESTION IS NOT WHETHER THE ELECTION CHANGED WASHINGTON. IT DID.

THE QUESTION IS WHETHER THE NEXT DECISION CHANGES THE WAR—AND WHAT EVIDENCE JUSTIFIES THAT DECISION.

THE EVIDENCE IS YOURS. THE CONCLUSIONS ARE YOURS.

TruthMatters News

Facts First. Analysis Second. Solutions Third.

Humans Create. AI Enhances. Humans Decide.

$PLNT Q3 2026 earnings: Planet Fitness lifts its sales plan, but franchisees build less

Planet Fitness beat its cautious sales plan at older gyms, but franchisees slowed new gym builds and membership stood still. Third-quarter revenue at the fitness chain and franchisor rose 9%, or 6% by our math excluding a pass-through advertising fee hike, as same-club sales edged up 1.5% and replacement machine orders carried the equipment unit. Chief executive Colleen Keating raised the full-year sales outlook, yet net profit excluding one-offs fell 8% on higher interest bills while total membership stayed at 21.5 million for a second quarter.

• Revenue (excluding ad-fund pass-through): $𝟑𝟔𝟎.𝟎𝐌 (+𝟔.𝟐% 𝐞𝐱-𝐚𝐝 𝐟𝐮𝐧𝐝) (+9.0% headline from a year ago)
• System-wide same-club sales: +𝟏.𝟓% (+6.9% a year ago; FY outlook raised to 1.5%–2%)
• Profit per share, excluding one-offs: $𝟎.𝟖𝟑 (+𝟑.𝟖%) (net profit excluding one-offs fell 7.6%)
• Franchisee new equipment placements plan: 𝐂𝐮𝐭 𝐭𝐨 𝟏𝟑𝟓–𝟏𝟒𝟎 (previously 150–160 for FY26)

⚖️ 𝐕𝐞𝐫𝐝𝐢𝐜𝐭: 🔴 Bearish

The story got worse because independent franchisees are building fewer gyms than planned, weakening the unit-growth engine that was supposed to carry the company while member growth is stalled. Management cut its full-year target for franchisee equipment placements by about 10% and only raised its club-opening target by counting 25 gyms it just bought in Portugal, which means underlying openings fell by 15 to 20 clubs by our math. One positive: the chain entered Portugal for $115 million and started a review to sell US company-owned gyms to franchisees.

The question now is whether the new marketing campaign and $10 promotional rate can restart member growth without cutting what each member pays. Either the January sign-up season brings in new members while keeping Black Card upgrades steady, or discounted sign-ups lower average dues just as last year's equipment boom fades. First-quarter membership additions and same-club sales will settle it.

Full article with charts - link in bio

🐂 𝐁𝐮𝐥𝐥 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🟢 𝐒𝐚𝐦𝐞-𝐂𝐥𝐮𝐛 𝐒𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬 𝐁𝐞𝐚𝐭 𝐚 𝐂𝐚𝐮𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐮𝐬 𝐏𝐥𝐚𝐧
Planet Fitness, the gym chain and franchisor, entered the second half with a full-year outlook that pointed to flat or negative same-club sales, by our math. Same-club sales measure monthly dues at gyms open more than a year. In the third quarter, system-wide same-club sales rose 1.5%, topping that implied range against a 6.9% gain a year ago.

Chief executive Colleen Keating said the chain "delivered same club sales growth ahead of our expectations" and lifted the full-year same-club target to 1.5% to 2%, up from 1%. That beat proves the prior outlook was cautious rather than proving member sign-ups have recovered, because total membership stayed at 21.5 million for a second straight quarter.

What to watch: fourth-quarter same-club sales, where the updated full-year target points to about 0.3% growth by our math. A result above 1% would show dues per member can hold up even before the January sign-up season.

🟢 𝐏𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐮𝐠𝐚𝐥 𝐃𝐞𝐚𝐥 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐂𝐥𝐮𝐛 𝐑𝐞𝐯𝐢𝐞𝐰 𝐒𝐡𝐢𝐟𝐭 𝐂𝐚𝐩𝐢𝐭𝐚𝐥
Planet Fitness runs about 10% of its gyms itself and franchises the rest to independent owners. Its strategy is to buy or build gyms in new markets, prove the model, and later sell those locations to franchisees so it can reuse the cash. This quarter the company advanced both ends of that plan.

In the fourth quarter it closed the purchase of Be-Fit, a Portuguese chain of 25 gyms with about 80,000 members, for roughly $114.8 million (€102.5 million). Keating said the deal gives the brand an "established national presence" in its second European country and should add to earnings in 2027. Separately, the board began a "strategic review of refranchising opportunities of its domestic corporate-owned clubs" to free up cash.

What to watch: the number of US corporate gyms put up for sale and the cash proceeds named on the fourth-quarter call. Selling US gyms would recoup the $112 million cash paid at closing for Portugal.

🟢 𝐏𝐨𝐬𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐯𝐞𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐪𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐝𝐢𝐝𝐧'𝐭 𝐭𝐞𝐬𝐭
Three operating drivers got no new numbers in the earnings release because their metrics live on the conference call or in the quarterly filing.

• Black Card membership share: the share of members on the higher-priced $24.99 tier stood at 68% last quarter; the call remarks will show if it rose again.
• Marketing and app relaunch: the redesigned mobile app, automated ad tool, and 100-day retention programme launched in September; first-quarter sign-ups are the first real test.
• Spa and recovery equipment: franchisees have been adding red-light and wellness amenities; the call will show how many clubs added them beyond the 100-club test.

🐻 𝐁𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🔴🔴 𝐅𝐫𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐡𝐢𝐬𝐞𝐞𝐬 𝐒𝐥𝐨𝐰 𝐍𝐞𝐰 𝐆𝐲𝐦 𝐎𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐢𝐧𝐠𝐬 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐎𝐫𝐝𝐞𝐫𝐬
Planet Fitness relies on independent franchisees to open roughly 90% of its new gyms and buy the exercise machines inside them. On the headline, the company raised its full-year target for system-wide new club openings to 190 to 195 locations, up from 180 to 190.

The footnote cuts against that raise: the new target is the first one "which includes the acquisition of Be-Fit" and its 25 existing gyms in Portugal. Stripping out those 25 bought gyms, underlying new openings fell to 165 to 170 by our math, a cut of 15 to 20 clubs. At the same time, the company cut its outlook for new equipment placements in franchisee gyms from 150 to 160 down to 135 to 140, after placing machines in 21 new franchisee gyms this quarter versus 27 a year ago.

What to watch: fourth-quarter franchisee equipment placements, which by our math must reach 80 to 85 to hit the lowered plan, compared with 96 in last year's fourth quarter. Another shortfall would show franchisees are delaying builds into 2027.

🔴🔴 𝐀𝐝-𝐅𝐮𝐧𝐝 𝐏𝐚𝐬𝐬-𝐓𝐡𝐫𝐨𝐮𝐠𝐡 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐑𝐞𝐩𝐥𝐚𝐜𝐞𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐬 𝐂𝐚𝐫𝐫𝐲 𝐑𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞
Total revenue rose 9.0% from a year ago to $360.0 million, but two low-margin or temporary items did most of the work. Starting in 2026, franchisees raised their contribution to the National Advertising Fund (NAF), the pool of money spent on national commercials, from 2% of sales to 3%. Because Planet Fitness records every dollar collected as revenue and every dollar spent as an identical expense, the change adds revenue with zero profit.

• Revenue excluding the ad fund: up 6.2% from a year ago by our math, 2.8 percentage points below the 9.0% headline.
• Operating margin: fell 4.2 percentage points to 28.2%, as ad-fund expense rose 2.4 percentage points of revenue and last year included a $6.4 million club-sale gain.
• Equipment revenue: up $8.8 million (11.1%), driven by $9.6 million more in replacement machines for older gyms while sales to new gyms fell $0.8 million.

What to watch: fourth-quarter revenue, where the raised 8% full-year outlook still implies a 2.3% drop from a year ago by our math, or a 5.4% drop excluding the ad fund, as the chain laps last year's record equipment quarter.

🔴 𝐅𝐥𝐚𝐭 𝐌𝐞𝐦𝐛𝐞𝐫𝐬𝐡𝐢𝐩 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐇𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐃𝐞𝐛𝐭 𝐖𝐞𝐢𝐠𝐡 𝐨𝐧 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐟𝐢𝐭
Planet Fitness ended September with approximately 21.5 million members, unchanged from both March and June. While the third quarter is seasonally slow for gym sign-ups, the member count has now gone six months without growing, leaving price mix and new gyms as the only drivers of dues.

Meanwhile, borrowing costs are taking a larger bite out of earnings. Gross interest expense rose 29.6% from a year ago to $34.1 million, and the $75.0 million credit line drawn in the second quarter to buy back shares remains on the balance sheet alongside $2.47 billion of other debt. As a result, net income excluding one-offs fell 7.6% to $61.9 million, and only a 10.7% drop in diluted shares kept profit per share excluding one-offs up 3.8% at $0.83. The board still approved a new $500 million buyback plan.

What to watch: whether management pays off the $75.0 million credit line by December as previously planned, especially after spending $112.0 million in cash to close the Portugal acquisition in the fourth quarter.

🔴 𝐑𝐢𝐬𝐤𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐪𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐝𝐢𝐝𝐧'𝐭 𝐚𝐧𝐬𝐰𝐞𝐫
Four standing risks around pricing, competition, and franchisee health received no new data in the earnings release.

• National $10 Classic Card promotion: no numbers on how many people joined on the discounted lifetime rate or whether they traded down from the $24.99 Black Card.
• Gross member sign-ups and cancellations: total membership stayed at 21.5 million, but the release does not split out how many joined versus cancelled.
• Regional price gaps: no update on South Central and Southeast markets where rival gyms charge less than the standard $15 Classic rate.
• Franchisee loans and credit reserves: the nine-month cash flow statement shows $20.6 million lent to a related party, and the credit-loss reserve on held-to-maturity investments ticked up $0.5 million to $26.0 million; the quarterly filing notes will give the details.

— • — • —

💲 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐊𝐏𝐈𝐬

𝐓𝐡𝐢𝐫𝐝-𝐪𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐜𝐚𝐩𝐢𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐞𝐱𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐞𝐬 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐟𝐫𝐞𝐞 𝐜𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐟𝐥𝐨𝐰 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟖𝟏.𝟓𝐌 𝐜𝐚𝐩𝐞𝐱 / $𝟐𝟖.𝟗𝐌 𝐅𝐂𝐅  ⇘ decelerating
Free cash flow — operating cash left after paying for buildings and gym equipment — dropped 62.6% from a year ago to $28.9 million in the third quarter, by our math from the nine-month cash flow statement. Capital spending jumped 48.8% in the quarter to $81.5 million as the chain built 8 corporate gyms and upgraded existing locations.

𝐃𝐞𝐟𝐞𝐫𝐫𝐞𝐝 𝐫𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐞𝐪𝐮𝐢𝐩𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐝𝐞𝐩𝐨𝐬𝐢𝐭𝐬 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟗𝟗.𝟒𝐌 / $𝟐𝟑.𝟎𝐌  ⇗ accelerating
Deferred revenue — cash collected up front for annual membership and franchise fees before the service is provided — rose 12.7% from December to $99.4 million. Equipment deposits from franchisees waiting for fourth-quarter machine deliveries more than doubled from December's $10.2 million to $23.0 million, backing the seasonal fourth-quarter installation wave.

𝐂𝐨𝐫𝐩𝐨𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐞-𝐨𝐰𝐧𝐞𝐝 𝐜𝐥𝐮𝐛𝐬 𝐒𝐞𝐠𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐀𝐝𝐣𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐄𝐁𝐈𝐓𝐃𝐀 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟓𝟑.𝟓 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
Profit before interest, taxes, and depreciation at company-run gyms edged down 0.4% from a year ago, even as segment sales rose 3.5% to $142.7 million on a 1.8% same-club sales gain. Operating costs at newly opened gyms ($1.9 million) and the August 2025 sale of eight California gyms ($1.0 million) offset gains at older locations.

— • — • —

🔮 𝐆𝐮𝐢𝐝𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟔 𝐒𝐲𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐦-𝐰𝐢𝐝𝐞 𝐬𝐚𝐦𝐞 𝐜𝐥𝐮𝐛 𝐬𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬 𝐠𝐫𝐨𝐰𝐭𝐡: ~𝟏.𝟓% 𝐭𝐨 𝟐%  ⇘ decelerating
🠅 raised from ~1%
Raised. The full-year target moved up by three-quarters of a point at the middle of the range after three straight quarters above 1%. By our math, with the first three quarters averaging 2.2%, the new range leaves roughly 0.3% same-club sales growth for the fourth quarter against a 5.7% gain a year ago. That keeps the fourth quarter positive after the company cut this target from 4%–5% in the spring.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟔 𝐑𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞 𝐠𝐫𝐨𝐰𝐭𝐡: ~𝟖%  ⇘ decelerating
🠅 raised from ~7%
Raised. The fitness franchisor lifted its top-line growth target by one percentage point, reversing half of the two-point cut it made in the first quarter. Because revenue already grew 12.1% over the first nine months, the 8% full-year plan points to fourth-quarter revenue of about $368 million by our math — down 2.3% from last year's fourth quarter, or down 5.4% excluding the ad-fund rate increase.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟔 𝐀𝐝𝐣𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐄𝐁𝐈𝐓𝐃𝐀 𝐠𝐫𝐨𝐰𝐭𝐡: ~𝟔.𝟓%  ⇒ stable
🠅 raised from ~6%
Raised. Operating cash profit before interest, taxes, and depreciation is now set to grow 6.5% this year, up half a point from the prior plan after growing 8.2% over the first nine months. By our math, that leaves about $149 million for the fourth quarter, or 1.7% growth from a year ago, as fourth-quarter equipment sales face a high comparison.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟔 𝐍𝐞𝐰 𝐞𝐪𝐮𝐢𝐩𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐩𝐥𝐚𝐜𝐞𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐬 𝐢𝐧 𝐟𝐫𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐡𝐢𝐬𝐞𝐞-𝐨𝐰𝐧𝐞𝐝 𝐥𝐨𝐜𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬: ~𝟏𝟑𝟓 𝐭𝐨 𝟏𝟒𝟎  ⇘ decelerating
🠇 cut from 150 to 160
Cut. The company lowered its expectation for new franchisee gym outfit orders by 17.5 locations at the middle of the range, down 10% from the 152 placements completed in 2025. With 56 placements finished through September (35 in the first half and 21 in the third quarter), the lowered plan leaves 79 to 84 placements for the fourth quarter against 96 a year ago.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟔 𝐒𝐲𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐦-𝐰𝐢𝐝𝐞 𝐧𝐞𝐰 𝐜𝐥𝐮𝐛 𝐨𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐢𝐧𝐠𝐬: ~𝟏𝟗𝟎 𝐭𝐨 𝟏𝟗𝟓 (𝐢𝐧𝐜𝐥𝐮𝐝𝐞𝐬 𝐁𝐞-𝐅𝐢𝐭)  ⇘ decelerating
🠅 raised from 180 to 190
Raised on the headline, cut underneath. Adding the 25 acquired Be-Fit gyms in Portugal lifted the stated range by 7.5 clubs at the middle, but excluding that purchase reduces underlying openings to 165 to 170 — down from 181 opened in 2025. With 71 gyms opened through September, the plan requires 94 to 99 fourth-quarter openings besides Be-Fit, compared with 104 last year.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟔 𝐂𝐚𝐩𝐢𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐞𝐱𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐞𝐬 𝐠𝐫𝐨𝐰𝐭𝐡: ~𝟏𝟓%  ⇘ decelerating
🠅 raised from ~10% to 15%
Raised to the top of the prior range. Full-year capital spending is now set to rise about 15% from last year's $163.7 million, or to roughly $188 million by our math. Because the US company already spent $148.9 million over the first nine months (up 31.1%), the full-year figure implies fourth-quarter capital spending drops to about $39 million from $50.1 million a year ago.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟔 𝐃𝐞𝐩𝐫𝐞𝐜𝐢𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐚𝐦𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐢𝐳𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐠𝐫𝐨𝐰𝐭𝐡: ~𝟕%  ⇒ stable
🠇 cut from ~10%
Cut. Expected growth in non-cash wear-and-tear and intangible write-downs dropped by three percentage points, matching the slower pace of corporate equipment and club additions through the first nine months, when the line rose 5.3% to $122.0 million. The lower non-cash charge helps cushion full-year net income against higher interest bills.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟔 𝐀𝐝𝐣𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐧𝐞𝐭 𝐢𝐧𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐞 𝐠𝐫𝐨𝐰𝐭𝐡: 𝐃𝐞𝐜𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐬𝐞 ~𝟑%  ⇘ decelerating
🠆 unchanged from Decrease ~3%
Unchanged. Even with higher revenue and EBITDA targets, the plan still has full-year profit excluding one-offs falling 3% to about $250.6 million by our math, after cutting this line in both the first and second quarters. Since nine-month profit excluding one-offs is roughly flat (+0.1% at $189.8 million), the full-year target points to a 12.0% drop in the fourth quarter.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟔 𝐀𝐝𝐣𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐧𝐞𝐭 𝐢𝐧𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐞 𝐩𝐞𝐫 𝐬𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞, 𝐝𝐢𝐥𝐮𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐠𝐫𝐨𝐰𝐭𝐡: ~𝟔% (𝐨𝐧 ~𝟕𝟕.𝟎𝐌 𝐬𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞𝐬)  ⇘ decelerating
🠆 unchanged from ~6% (on ~77.0M shares)
Unchanged. Profit per share excluding one-offs is still set to rise 6% for the year, entirely because share buybacks cut the average share count from 84.1 million last year to about 77.0 million. The third-quarter share count already reached 75.0 million after the latest $50.0 million buyback, leaving a small per-share cushion for the fourth quarter.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟔 𝐍𝐞𝐭 𝐢𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐭 𝐞𝐱𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐬𝐞: ~$𝟏𝟏𝟓.𝟎 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇒ stable
🠆 unchanged from ~$115.0 million
Unchanged. Net interest cost stays at the $115.0 million level set last quarter after the company drew $75.0 million on its variable funding notes. Through nine months, gross interest expense minus interest income totaled $84.4 million, leaving about $30.6 million of net interest cost for the fourth quarter versus $24.0 million in last year's fourth quarter.

— • — • —

❓ 𝐊𝐞𝐲 𝐐𝐮𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬

𝐃𝐢𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐞 $𝟏𝟎 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐦𝐨𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐥𝐢𝐟𝐭 𝐬𝐢𝐠𝐧-𝐮𝐩𝐬 𝐨𝐫 𝐜𝐮𝐭 𝐩𝐫𝐢𝐜𝐞𝐬?
Planet Fitness tested a national $10 monthly Classic Card offer in the third quarter with lifetime price protection, yet total membership stayed at 21.5 million. Management has not disclosed how many members joined on the $10 rate or how many skipped the $24.99 Black Card.

𝐖𝐡𝐲 𝐝𝐢𝐝 𝐟𝐫𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐡𝐢𝐬𝐞𝐞𝐬 𝐝𝐞𝐥𝐚𝐲 𝟏𝟓 𝐭𝐨 𝟐𝟎 𝐧𝐞𝐰 𝐠𝐲𝐦𝐬?
Cutting franchisee equipment placements from 150–160 to 135–140 while masking the drop in the club-opening target with 25 bought gyms in Portugal points to slower franchisee building. Investors need to know whether real estate delays, equipment costs, or weaker club returns caused the slip.

𝐇𝐨𝐰 𝐦𝐚𝐧𝐲 𝐔𝐒 𝐜𝐨𝐫𝐩𝐨𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐞 𝐠𝐲𝐦𝐬 𝐜𝐨𝐮𝐥𝐝 𝐛𝐞 𝐬𝐨𝐥𝐝?
The company owns roughly 10% of its nearly 3,000 clubs and just opened a strategic review to sell domestic corporate gyms to franchisees. Naming the number of clubs under review and the EBITDA they generate would show how much cash the review can unlock.

𝐖𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐭𝐡𝐞 $𝟕𝟓𝐌 𝐜𝐫𝐞𝐝𝐢𝐭 𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐞 𝐛𝐞 𝐫𝐞𝐩𝐚𝐢𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐲𝐞𝐚𝐫?
Last quarter the finance chief planned to repay the $75.0 million variable funding note from cash by December. That loan was still on the balance sheet on September 30, just before Planet Fitness paid $112.0 million in cash at closing for Be-Fit in Portugal.

𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐫𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐟𝐢𝐭 𝐧𝐮𝐦𝐛𝐞𝐫𝐬 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐁𝐞-𝐅𝐢𝐭?
Planet Fitness paid €102.5 million ($114.8 million) for 25 gyms and 80,000 members in Portugal and said the deal will add to earnings in 2027, without giving Be-Fit's annual sales, EBITDA, or the cost to convert the clubs to the Planet Fitness brand.

EARLY MORNING DISPATCH UPDATE
THURSDAY, NOVEMBER 5, 2026

Overnight dispatch activity across the Denver metro area included reports of assaults, possible firearm incidents, a vehicle crashing through a residential yard, a pedestrian reportedly struck by a vehicle, multiple hit-and-run collisions, a vehicle fire, medical emergencies, and transit disturbances.

Reports cover the evening of November 4 through approximately 4:03 a.m. November 5.

JEFFERSON COUNTY, LAKEWOOD, ARVADA AND WEST METRO

ARVADA | NOISE COMPLAINT AT ARVADA RIDGE
4:03 AM | Arvada Ridge parking lot

Police responded to a report of loud music and shouting in the Arvada Ridge parking lot. One unit requested an area check while another offered assistance. No final outcome was available.

ARVADA | ASSAULT REPORTED AT APARTMENT COMPLEX
3:56 AM | West 52nd Avenue, near Carr Street and Cody Street

Emergency personnel were dispatched to a reported assault at an apartment complex near West 52nd Avenue. Injuries and arrest information were not confirmed.

ARVADA | VEHICLE CRASHES THROUGH YARD AND HITS TREE
3:28 AM | Wadsworth Boulevard

Fire crews responded after a vehicle reportedly traveled through a residential yard and struck a tree. Police were already on scene, and responding personnel were checking for injuries.

ARVADA | POSSIBLE FUMES REPORTED
3:17 AM | West 86th Avenue

A caller reported smelling possible fumes across the street before leaving the area. The source was not established.

LAKEWOOD AREA | SMOKE INVESTIGATION
2:51 AM | West 16th Avenue and Sheridan Boulevard

Fire crews were dispatched to investigate possible smoke near the intersection. No confirmed fire was reported in the available information.

KEN CARYL | RECKLESS DRIVER ON C-470
11:38 PM | Eastbound C-470 near Ken Caryl Avenue

Dispatch received a report of a red sedan weaving through traffic and traveling at excessive speed. The vehicle was last reported continuing eastbound. No traffic stop was confirmed.

RED ROCKS | MEDICAL RESPONSE FOR POSSIBLY IMPAIRED PATRON
11:07 PM | Red Rocks Park and Amphitheatre, 18300 West Alameda Parkway, Morrison

Medics responded to the Eastgate area for a possibly impaired patron. A medical unit arrived on scene. The patient's condition was not provided.

LAKEWOOD | POSSIBLE INDECENT EXPOSURE
10:46 PM | Junction 3, west stairwell

Transit dispatch received a report of possible indecent exposure in a west-side stairwell at a facility identified as Junction 3. Assistance was requested. The precise location and outcome were not independently confirmed.

LAKEWOOD | I-70 LANE CLOSURE FOR POTHOLE REPAIRS
9:28 PM | Westbound I-70 near Colorado Mills and Colfax Avenue

Transportation dispatch described a planned closure of the number three lane for pothole repairs. Traffic was being diverted around the work area. The closure's current status is unknown.

DENVER

DOWNTOWN | POLICE SEARCH FOR ASSAULT SUSPECT
3:35 AM | 16th Street

Police radio traffic described a search for a possible assault suspect, reportedly a young adult man with a thin build and blond hair, wearing a black shirt and black jeans. Dispatch indicated he might be traveling toward Union Station or Littleton. No apprehension was confirmed.

NORTHEAST DENVER | TWO PEOPLE REPORTED UNRESPONSIVE IN ELEVATOR
2:58 AM | East 40th Avenue and Colorado Boulevard

Security requested assistance after finding two people reportedly sleeping in an elevator and not responding to attempts to wake them. Their medical conditions were not confirmed.

NORTH DENVER | GUN-RELATED POLICE RESPONSE
2:31 AM | North Downing Street

Dispatch referenced a call involving a firearm. Officers were directed to another radio channel. Further details were unavailable in the monitored dispatch information.

DENVER | DOMESTIC DISTURBANCE INVOLVING REPORTED GUN
2:20 AM | East 39th Avenue

Police were dispatched to a possible domestic disturbance involving a firearm at a residence. Injuries, arrests and whether a firearm was recovered were not confirmed.

SOUTHWEST DENVER | HIT-AND-RUN FOLLOW-UP
1:55 AM | South Hooker Street

Police followed up on a reported collision near South Lowell Boulevard and West Quincy Avenue. Dispatch referenced a person reportedly fleeing on foot and a silver sedan leaving the area. No arrest was confirmed.

DENVER | TRESPASSING RESPONSE
12:05 AM | 13th Street

Officers responded to a possible trespassing incident. Dispatch information indicated a person was escorted from the property.

WEST COLFAX | BUS STRUCK IN HIT-AND-RUN
11:20 PM | West Colfax Avenue and Perry Street

Transit radio traffic reported that a turning vehicle struck a bus and left the scene. No injuries were reported. Additional traffic discussed arranging another vehicle to pick up passengers.

A notable development for $ALOY REalloys and the U.S. Army have signed a non binding term sheet for a potential heavy rare-earth processing facility at Tooele Army Depot in Utah.

The proposed site covers about 200 acres. The term sheet outlines a possible 50 year lease with one 25 year renewal option, and gives the Army a right of first offer to purchase product. The Army is not obligated to buy, and the parties still need to negotiate a definitive lease and satisfy conditions that include permitting, financing and environmental review.

It’s a significant proposal to follow, but it remains under negotiation. The next milestone is whether the parties can complete a definitive agreement and move the project toward development.

text:
$PRKS Q3 2026 earnings: United Parks attendance falls again, but season pass sales rebound

Fewer people visited United Parks, the operator of SeaWorld and Busch Gardens, during its peak summer quarter, though guests who came spent more and season pass sales turned up. Attendance fell 5% from a year ago, pulling revenue down 1% to $506 million and net profit down 10% to $80 million. Chief executive Marc Swanson blamed bad weather, calendar shifts, and weaker international tourism for 325,000 lost visits, and noted that cutting promotional tickets cost another 100,000.

• Park attendance: 𝟔.𝟒𝟕𝐌 (-4.7% from a year ago)
• Total spending per guest: $𝟕𝟖.𝟐𝟗 (+3.8% from a year ago)
• Upfront cash for passes and tickets: $𝟏𝟓𝟐.𝟒𝐌 (+4.7% from a year ago)
• 2027 season pass base (Oct 31): 𝐍𝐞𝐰 𝐨𝐮𝐭𝐥𝐨𝐨𝐤 (up over 15% from a year ago)

⚖️ 𝐕𝐞𝐫𝐝𝐢𝐜𝐭: ⚪ Neutral

The standing story is unchanged because rising advance bookings and guest spending are still fighting a multi-year slide in foot traffic and climbing overhead costs. On the bright side, upfront customer deposits grew 5% by our math, average ticket prices stopped falling, and the total paid pass base finally turned positive in October. The bad news: park traffic dropped against an easy comparison from last year, corporate overhead jumped 13%, and free cash flow fell while $40 million stays drawn on the credit line.

The question now is whether the 15% jump in early 2027 season pass sales will actually bring more people through the turnstiles, or merely raise prices on a shrinking crowd as Orlando competition intensifies. If the larger pass base drives real volume, attendance will grow without heavy discounting; if regional awareness and rival parks are the real problem, foot traffic will stay negative. Fourth-quarter holiday attendance and the year-end pass base will tell.

Full article with charts - link in bio

🐂 𝐁𝐮𝐥𝐥 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🟢🟢 𝐀𝐝𝐯𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞 𝐓𝐢𝐜𝐤𝐞𝐭 𝐒𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐏𝐚𝐬𝐬 𝐁𝐚𝐬𝐞 𝐓𝐮𝐫𝐧𝐞𝐝 𝐏𝐨𝐬𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐯𝐞
Deferred revenue is cash customers have paid upfront for season passes and future park visits. Because pass holders account for about two-fifths of all visits at United Parks, the operator of SeaWorld and Busch Gardens, this upfront balance is the clearest indicator of future park traffic.

After shrinking throughout 2025, the upfront cash balance rose 4.7% from a year ago to $152.4 million, accelerating from 2.0% growth in the second quarter. Chief executive Marc Swanson said "our total pass sales during the third quarter were up almost 8% and our total paid pass base was positive as of October 31st", reversing a year of shrinking pass-holder counts.

• Deferred revenue: $152.4 million, up 4.7% from a year ago by our math
• 2027 pass product base: "up over 15% as of October 31st", according to Swanson
• 2027 bookings for Discovery Cove and group events: "running up double digit percentages versus prior year at the same time"

This upturn matters because a growing base of pass holders locks in recurring visitors for the next twelve months. Even when bad weather washed out parts of October, total revenue for the month rose from a year ago and Halloween events grew on dry days.

What to watch: the year-end deferred revenue balance and pass-holder count after the Black Friday selling season. Holding a positive pass base through December would confirm that advance demand can lift attendance in 2027.

🟢 𝐆𝐮𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐬 𝐒𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐌𝐨𝐫𝐞 𝐨𝐧 𝐁𝐨𝐭𝐡 𝐓𝐢𝐜𝐤𝐞𝐭𝐬 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐏𝐚𝐫𝐤 𝐄𝐱𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐬
United Parks tracks revenue per capita, which is the average amount each guest spends on entry tickets (admission per capita) and on food, merchandise and upgrades inside the gates (in-park per capita). For over a year, promotions and discounting dragged down average ticket prices even as food and merchandise spending climbed.

In the third quarter, the theme park group intentionally cut back on promotional ticket offers, sacrificing more than 100,000 low-paying visits. That trade-off lifted average ticket spending by 3.4% from a year ago to $40.90, while average spending inside the parks rose 4.4% to a record $37.39. Together, total spending per guest rose 3.8% to $78.29, almost offsetting the drop in headcount.

What to watch: admission spending per guest in the fourth quarter as more pass holders visit for holiday events. Because frequent pass visits lower the average price per entry, keeping ticket yields positive would prove that firmer pricing is sticking.

🟢 𝐒𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐁𝐮𝐲𝐛𝐚𝐜𝐤𝐬 𝐓𝐮𝐫𝐧𝐞𝐝 𝐚 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐟𝐢𝐭 𝐃𝐫𝐨𝐩 𝐈𝐧𝐭𝐨 𝐏𝐞𝐫-𝐒𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐆𝐫𝐨𝐰𝐭𝐡
Heavy share repurchases over the past year have shrunk the share count, which boosts profit per share for remaining owners, though bears point out those buybacks drained cash and required credit-line borrowing. By our math, diluted shares fell 17.1% from a year ago to 46.0 million, and dropped 1.2 million shares from the second quarter alone.

That smaller denominator turned a 10.5% drop in third-quarter net income ($80.0 million) into an 8.1% increase in diluted earnings per share ($1.74). At the same time, cash ended September at just $26.3 million with $40.0 million still drawn on the revolving credit line, down from $50.0 million in June. By our math, net debt sits at $2.25 billion, or 3.9 times trailing twelve-month Adjusted EBITDA (3.55 times using the lender formula that adds $46.0 million of future cost savings).

What to watch: exact third-quarter share repurchase spending in the upcoming quarterly filing. Because free cash flow fell 38.3% from a year ago to $23.5 million, further buybacks in the slow fourth quarter would require borrowing more on the credit line.

🐻 𝐁𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🔴🔴 𝐏𝐚𝐫𝐤 𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐞𝐧𝐝𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞 𝐅𝐞𝐥𝐥 𝐀𝐠𝐚𝐢𝐧𝐬𝐭 𝐚𝐧 𝐄𝐚𝐬𝐲 𝐂𝐨𝐦𝐩𝐚𝐫𝐢𝐬𝐨𝐧
"Excluding the impact of these unusual headwinds, which amounted to approximately 325,000 visits, our attendance would have been up," chief executive Marc Swanson said. Swanson blamed bad weather, calendar shifts, and fewer overseas tourists for the drop, repeating an explanation management has given for over a year.

The numbers from this quarter and last year cut against that framing. Reported attendance fell 4.7%, or 320,000 guests, to 6.47 million, marking the eighth decline in the last nine quarters. Worse, this quarter already lapped an easy comparison from the third quarter of 2025, when the Florida-based group lost about 240,000 visits to a Fourth of July calendar shift and weaker international travel.

Even adding back all 325,000 visits Swanson cited would leave traffic up less than 0.1% by our math against last year's depressed base, while deliberately cutting promotional tickets cost another 100,000 visits. When traffic falls in eight of nine quarters, weather and calendar quirks no longer explain the trend, pointing instead to stiffer competition in Orlando and weaker awareness at regional parks.

What to watch: fourth-quarter attendance during the holiday events. Because the fourth quarter of 2025 also suffered from bad weather and fewer operating days, another decline would confirm that park traffic faces structural pressure.

🔴 𝐎𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐡𝐞𝐚𝐝 𝐂𝐨𝐬𝐭𝐬 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐀𝐝𝐝-𝐁𝐚𝐜𝐤𝐬 𝐊𝐞𝐞𝐩 𝐑𝐢𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐠
United Parks set a target of $50 million in gross cost savings for 2026 to protect its profit margins. While park operating expenses (the direct cost of running rides and caring for animals) fell 1.9% from a year ago in the third quarter, corporate overhead moved the wrong way.

Selling, general and administrative expenses — marketing and corporate overhead — jumped 13.1% from a year ago to $68.6 million, rising 1.7 percentage points to 13.5% of revenue by our math. That overhead increase pulled operating margin down 1.9 percentage points to 27.8%. Meanwhile, the company excluded $12.4 million of business optimization and legal adjustment costs from Adjusted EBITDA ($205.1 million, down 5.1%), more than double the $5.6 million excluded a year ago.

What to watch: selling, general and administrative expenses and optimization add-backs in the fourth quarter. If corporate overhead and excluded charges stay elevated at year-end, inflation and consulting fees are eating up the promised cost savings.

🔴 𝐑𝐢𝐬𝐤𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐪𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐝𝐢𝐝𝐧'𝐭 𝐚𝐧𝐬𝐰𝐞𝐫
Several standing items from prior quarters received no update in the third-quarter earnings release because they typically appear on the conference call or in the quarterly filing.

• Real estate bids and sale-leaseback risk: no update on third-party offers for company land or how new rent obligations would lower ongoing profit.
• Sesame Workshop license lawsuit: no mention in the release; the quarterly filing's legal footnotes will show any progress in the dispute covering the two Sesame Place parks.
• Regional park awareness and marketing: no breakdown of traffic at Busch Gardens Tampa Bay versus Orlando parks; conference call commentary will address regional trends.

👓 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐓𝐡𝐞𝐦𝐞𝐬

𝐍𝐞𝐰 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟕 𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬 𝐔𝐧𝐯𝐞𝐢𝐥𝐞𝐝 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐅𝐥𝐨𝐫𝐢𝐝𝐚 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐕𝐢𝐫𝐠𝐢𝐧𝐢𝐚
United Parks unveiled its initial 2027 ride lineup to support season pass sales. SeaWorld Orlando will open SEAQuest: Legends of the Deep, "a vibrant submersible adventure through dazzling undersea ecosystems" delayed from an earlier 2026 schedule, while Busch Gardens Williamsburg will debut Return to Corkscrew Hill, "North America’s first-of-its-kind motion theater ride", and Tampa Bay will announce its attraction in two weeks.

— • — • —

💲 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐊𝐏𝐈𝐬

𝐂𝐚𝐩𝐢𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐞𝐱𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐞𝐬 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟔𝟗.𝟕 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
Capital spending rose 22.9% from a year ago to 13.8% of revenue, pulling nine-month spending up 24.3% to $207.9 million. By our math, third-quarter spending shifted toward expansion and return-on-investment projects ($22.4 million vs $10.2 million in the entire first half), leaving about $47 million of expansion spending for the fourth quarter under the prior full-year plan.

𝐅𝐨𝐨𝐝, 𝐦𝐞𝐫𝐜𝐡𝐚𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐬𝐞 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐨𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐫𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟐𝟒𝟏.𝟖 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
In-park revenue edged down 0.6% from a year ago after growing 2.0% in the second quarter, as the 4.7% drop in guest headcount outweighed the 4.4% increase in spending per guest. Even so, food and merchandise held up better than ticket admissions revenue, which fell 1.5% to $264.6 million.

— • — • —

🔮 𝐆𝐮𝐢𝐝𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞

𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟕 𝐃𝐢𝐬𝐜𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐲 𝐂𝐨𝐯𝐞 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐠𝐫𝐨𝐮𝐩 𝐛𝐨𝐨𝐤𝐢𝐧𝐠𝐬 𝐫𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞: 𝐔𝐩 𝐝𝐨𝐮𝐛𝐥𝐞-𝐝𝐢𝐠𝐢𝐭 𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐜𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐚𝐠𝐞𝐬 𝐘𝐨𝐘  ⇒ stable
🠆 unchanged from Up double-digits versus prior year
Unchanged. The theme park operator reiterated that advance booking revenue for its all-inclusive Discovery Cove resort and corporate group events is pacing up by double-digit percentages for 2027, matching the forward commentary given in the second quarter. Management gives no dollar figures or formal full-year revenue targets in the release.

𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟕 𝐬𝐩𝐞𝐜𝐢𝐟𝐢𝐜 𝐩𝐚𝐬𝐬 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐝𝐮𝐜𝐭 𝐛𝐚𝐬𝐞 (𝐚𝐬 𝐨𝐟 𝐎𝐜𝐭 𝟑𝟏): 𝐔𝐩 𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫 𝟏𝟓% 𝐘𝐨𝐘  ⇗ accelerating
New. Early unit sales of 2027 season passes are running more than 15% ahead of last year's pace through October 31, while total pass sales in the third quarter rose nearly 8% and pushed the overall paid pass base back into positive growth.

— • — • —

❓ 𝐊𝐞𝐲 𝐐𝐮𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬

𝐇𝐨𝐰 𝐦𝐮𝐜𝐡 𝐝𝐢𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐩𝐚𝐧𝐲 𝐬𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐝 𝐨𝐧 𝐐𝟑 𝐛𝐮𝐲𝐛𝐚𝐜𝐤𝐬?
Diluted shares fell by 1.2 million from the second quarter while free cash flow was only $23.5 million and $40 million remained drawn on the credit line. Investors need the exact repurchase outlay from the quarterly filing to judge balance-sheet strain.

𝐖𝐡𝐞𝐫𝐞 𝐝𝐨 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐫𝐝-𝐩𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐲 𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐥 𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐭𝐞 𝐛𝐢𝐝𝐬 𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐧𝐝?
Last quarter management highlighted strong outside interest in buying park land, but the third-quarter release gave no update. Selling land and leasing it back would add permanent rent bills that reduce ongoing operating cash flow.

𝐇𝐨𝐰 𝐦𝐮𝐜𝐡 𝐨𝐟 𝐭𝐡𝐞 $𝟓𝟎𝐌 𝐜𝐨𝐬𝐭 𝐬𝐚𝐯𝐢𝐧𝐠𝐬 𝐢𝐬 𝐨𝐟𝐟𝐬𝐞𝐭𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐡𝐞𝐚𝐝?
Selling, general and administrative expenses jumped 13.1% from a year ago in the third quarter, and optimization add-backs reached $25.4 million for the first nine months. Management has not disclosed how much net savings remain after inflation and consulting fees.

text:
History was made on Tuesday night, an ocean away, and I think it was made for us too.
For two years the American right told itself that anger was a governing strategy. 

On Tuesday the people who had been angry on its behalf voted it out of both houses of Congress and, for the first time since the early 1990s, out of every statewide office in Texas. Ted Cruz, in his own post-mortem, called it a Watergate-level repudiation. Sometimes history is celebrated. Sometimes it is mourned. 

Reform UK has spent two years copying the playbook that just failed.
Start with what beat them, in their own numbers. Cruz's exit polling from Kansas, a state that had not sent a Democrat to the Senate since 1932 and just did: cost of living first, by a mile. Corruption second. The cost of the Iran war third. "The candidates are terrible" fourth. The trade war fifth. Nothing from the culture war made the top five. The voters who swung were not converts. They were customers returning a product.

The OBR said last week that households will end this decade no better off than they started it. Energy bills rise by more than £450 in January and the Budget's answer was £100. Nearly three million emergency food parcels went out last year. 

Here is why I don't think it carries Nigel Farage to No.10, issue by issue, in the order the Americans just ranked them.

Cost of living. Reform's offer is a £15,000 personal allowance, 3% of GDP on defence and lower borrowing, in one breath. Voters have noticed. On economic trust Reform sits at 12%, behind Labour and the Conservatives on 21% each. You can win a protest with a slogan. You cannot survive a Budget with one.

Corruption.  In Britain, ITV spent a year inside Reform and filmed councillors calling their fellow citizens animals and a senior official saying the job was to defend the indefensible. The party's response was to report the journalists to the police. The American right just learned that voters forgive a great deal and do not forgive being taken for fools.

The candidates. Almost 8% of Kansans said theirs were terrible. Reform elected hundreds of councillors in a single afternoon in May 2025, and the footage speaks for them.

Young people. They voted Republican in 2024 and swung hard the other way by 2026. Reform's surge among young men here is the same soft vote, held by the same thing, which is that nothing has been asked of it yet.

So Reform's ceiling is where America's right just found its floor. The product is anger, and anger is a one-term product.

Cruz's lesson, which he credits to his wife, is that it is never about you. It's about their kids, their bills, their futures. The American right lost because it forgot that. The British centre will lose if it treats Tuesday as proof it was right. It proves only that anger changes sides. 

Labour's Budget last week was careful to the point of absence, and a government that answers a £450 bill with £100 is doing Reform's recruiting for it. The way to keep Farage out of No.10 is to make the anger unnecessary, which means taking the risks the Chancellor declined to take, on tax, on housing, on the things that cost people money every month.

Cruz closed by saying it is darkest before the dawn. Britain's problem is dullness rather than darkness, and dull is how populists win, slowly, while the centre congratulates itself on calm markets. Reform will not be in No.10 if the centre earns it. Tuesday was America's warning to its right. It should be read as Britain's warning to everyone else.

“We Are Sudanese Through and Through”: A Woman’s Cry from Taiba Exposes a Stark Contradiction — Our Sons Fight in the Army’s Ranks While the State Demolishes Our Homes!

5 November 2026 | The New Republic

🟥 “We Made You Celebrate and Restored You to the Homes You Had Fled. Is This How We Are Repaid?”

🟦 Our Sons Fight on the Front Lines, While Their Mothers Watch Their Homes Being Demolished by State Authorities!

⬛️ “We Are Sudanese Through and Through”: A Defiant Rejection of Racism — Who Protects Those Fighting to Defend Their Country?

In a deeply distressing video, a Sudanese woman from among the families affected by the demolition of homes in Taiba Al-Sheikh Abdul Baqi, north of Wad Madani in Al Jazirah State, delivers an anguished and impassioned message to the sons of Darfur, Kordofan and the Nuba Mountains who are fighting in the ranks of the Sudanese army. She urges them to return to their families, arguing that they are fighting to defend a state whose own institutions are demolishing their relatives’ homes and violating their dignity.

The woman was not speaking about a political disagreement or a military rivalry. She was speaking about a home she had watched being demolished before her eyes, and about sons and brothers who had left their homes to enlist in the army, believing they were defending their country, only for their families to find themselves confronting demolition operations carried out by the very state under whose banner their sons are fighting.

Her words amounted to a powerful moral and political indictment, capturing the contradiction experienced by segments of communities originating from western Sudan: participation in the army’s military campaigns on one hand, and exposure to exclusionary and discriminatory rhetoric — and even the loss of their homes in areas where their families have lived for decades — on the other.

🟥 “We Were Going to Fight Those Nuba ‘Slaves’”: The Incitement Rhetoric That Preceded the War

Among the most revealing aspects of the woman’s testimony is her account of what was allegedly said to her sons and brothers when the war began and they were being recruited to fight in the army’s ranks.

According to her account, the conflict was presented to them as a war against the Nuba people, using the explicitly racist expression: “We are going to fight those Nuba slaves all the way to Kauda.”

This raises serious concerns about the rhetoric allegedly used to mobilise some young men from Darfur, Kordofan and the Nuba Mountains. A conflict that should be understood in military and political terms is thereby transformed into an assault on entire communities on the basis of their ethnic and regional identities.

The contradiction is particularly striking: the same woman now speaks of her family’s exposure to discrimination and exclusion because of their origins, while her sons and brothers were allegedly sent to the battlefront under rhetoric targeting another ethnic community.

It is a dangerous cycle of racial incitement in which young men from marginalised communities are turned into fuel for the war, while their participation in military operations offers no guarantee that they or their families will enjoy protection or equal rights.

Eli Sharabi, an Israeli hostage who was held captive in Gaza, visited Bratislava and presented the Slovak translation of his book Hostage (Rukojemník).

491 days. That is how long Eli was held captive by Hamas. He was abducted from his home in Kibbutz Be’eri on 7 October 2023. For 491 days, Eli kept thinking about the promise he had made to his wife and two daughters as he was being taken away: I will come back. Throughout his captivity, Eli had no idea that terrorists had shot and killed his wife and two daughters just minutes after he was abducted.

It is not an easy book to read. It describes hunger, physical violence, humiliation, fear and the systematic stripping away of human dignity. But it also contains something profoundly important: a very concrete picture of the society in which he found himself.

For the first 50-plus days, he was held in the family home of an ordinary Gazan family. Everyday life carried on around him. The family ate together and spent time together, the children did their schoolwork, and the men prayed aloud. And one floor above, they kept an Israeli hostage bound and captive.

He was not guarded by uniformed soldiers. His captors had families of their own and civilian jobs.

Today, there is passionate debate about civilian casualties in Gaza. 
We often encounter an extremely simplified picture of the war: on one side, the Israeli army; on the other, innocent civilians. But where, exactly, does the terrorist organisation Hamas fit into this simplified picture?

The war in Gaza is not simply a fight against a clearly identifiable enemy wearing a uniform. 

Eli’s experience shows that someone who leads an ordinary civilian life during the day may also be keeping an Israeli hostage chained up in their home like a pet.

The dilemmas posed by this war in an urban environment are almost impossible to resolve.

How, for example, do you distinguish between an innocent child and a twelve-year-old boy who has undergone military training and knows how to fire an automatic weapon? Hamas deliberately blurs this line.

Since this terrorist organisation came to power in Gaza, it has committed many crimes. 

Yet there is one that is sometimes overlooked. Hamas has created and raised a generation of young, unfeeling human robots ready to kill at any moment. 
Through indoctrination, it has robbed children of their childhood.

Resolving this conflict is not a matter of a single war against terrorism. 

It is a multigenerational task of giving Gaza another sense of purpose in life, one that is not centred on the determination to kill. 

Peace cannot be built on the idea that hatred of Israel is a natural, understandable or even politically legitimate part of Palestinian identity. Palestinian children deserve education, security and a future.💯👍

The Middle East conflict is reflected here in Europe as well.

In the streets, on social media and at universities, young people are mobilising who see themselves as humanists and progressive anti-colonialists. 

Many of them have a sincere desire to fight injustice. But sincere idealism without knowledge of history and facts is easily exploited.💯👍

And radical movements take advantage of this. 

They offer a simple picture: Israel is evil, Palestine is good. Anyone who tries to explain anything more nuanced to them is subjected to the worst kinds of labels and threats.

Criticising the Israeli government is legitimate. There is little point in repeating the familiar fact that Israel is the only parliamentary democracy in the Middle East, lest it become a cliché. 

Analysing the effectiveness of military operations is legitimate and indeed necessary. 

But denying the Jewish people the right to a state of their own is neither progressive nor humanist.

text:
FORECAST VERIFICATION: HOW DID WE DO? I've been taking somewhat of a backseat when it comes to MY opinion on the current state of weather information on social media. I would be lying if I said it wasn't the wild, wild west out there, and frankly, I don't see that changing anytime soon. It's all fine and dandy until outrageous forecasts start getting shared daily, misinformation spreads, and people begin questioning who they can actually trust when significant weather threatens their communities.

So, I've been thinking about something I want to start doing more often here at Southern Tennessee Weather: forecast verification. After significant weather events, whether that's heavy rainfall, snowfall, severe thunderstorms, or something else, I want to take a look back at our forecasts and compare them to what actually happened. What did we get right? What did we get wrong? And what could we have done better? I believe having open and honest conversations about forecast accuracy, including acknowledging when we miss the mark, is one of the best ways to build trust. Meteorology isn't a perfect science, and no forecast will ever be 100% accurate, but that doesn't mean we shouldn't hold ourselves accountable for the information we share.

With that being said, let's take a look at our rainfall forecast from Tuesday night into Wednesday! Our forecast called for widespread rainfall totals of 1–2 inches across Southern Middle Tennessee, with localized amounts potentially reaching 3 inches. Looking at estimated rainfall totals from this event, I'm pleased to say our forecast verified quite nicely overall! Most of our coverage area picked up between 1–2 inches of rain, with some locations exceeding 3 inches, particularly in a swath extending from eastern Maury County through Marshall County and into western Bedford County.

Of course, there were a few places where our forecast didn't verify quite as well, especially across Franklin County, where rainfall totals were somewhat underwhelming compared to what we anticipated. A big reason for this was the final line of showers and thunderstorms becoming more broken and scattered as it approached the Alabama state line, leaving some communities with less rainfall than others. That's an important part of forecast verification, too. Just because a forecast works out well for most of the area doesn't mean it worked out equally well for everyone!

It's also worth mentioning that these are ESTIMATED rainfall totals, meaning they may not perfectly reflect what fell in your backyard. In fact, I've already received a few reports suggesting some of these estimates may be a little too low. Nevertheless, they give us a pretty good overall picture of how this event unfolded.

Now, the million-dollar question: Did this rain help our ongoing drought? Well, we're certainly heading in the right direction, but we won't get a clear picture from this week's U.S. Drought Monitor update. That's because the weekly analysis only incorporates conditions through Tuesday morning, meaning Wednesday's rainfall won't be reflected until next week's update. We've now had multiple rounds of beneficial rainfall in a relatively short period of time, which is encouraging after such an extended stretch of dry weather. However, drought recovery takes time, and we'll need more consistent rainfall to make substantial improvements.

Overall, I'm happy with how our rainfall forecast performed. We accurately captured the general range of rainfall across much of Southern Middle Tennessee, including the potential for localized totals exceeding 3 inches. There were a few areas where we overestimated rainfall, and those misses are just as important to acknowledge.

My goal with these forecast verifications isn't to pat ourselves on the back when we get something right. It's to be transparent about our forecasting process, learn from our mistakes, and help you better understand the science behind the forecasts you depend on. At the end of the day, trust isn't built by pretending to be right all the time. It's built through honesty, consistency, and accountability, and that's exactly what I want Southern Tennessee Weather to stand for! Have a GREAT start to your Thursday!

text:
Today in History 
November 5th 
1935
Parker Brothers Begins Marketing Monopoly

On November 5, 1935, Parker Brothers began marketing Monopoly, a board game that would become one of the most popular and recognizable games in history. Introduced during the Great Depression, Monopoly offered Americans an entertaining escape from economic hardship by allowing players to buy properties, build houses and hotels, collect rent, and accumulate imaginary fortunes.

The Origins of Monopoly
Although Monopoly became a commercial sensation in 1935, its origins date back more than three decades.

In 1903, American inventor and political activist Elizabeth Magie created The Landlord’s Game, which she patented in 1904. Inspired by economist Henry George, Magie designed the game to demonstrate the dangers of concentrated landownership, monopolies, and economic inequality.

Her original game included different sets of rules intended to illustrate how wealth could either become concentrated among a few individuals or benefit an entire community.

Over the following decades, the game spread through households, universities, and social circles. Players modified its rules and introduced new property names, gradually transforming it into the familiar game of real estate competition.

Charles Darrow and Parker Brothers
During the early 1930s, Charles Darrow, an unemployed salesman from Pennsylvania, encountered a version of the game and began producing his own sets.

Darrow’s version featured streets from Atlantic City, New Jersey, including Boardwalk, Park Place, and Baltic Avenue.

He initially approached Parker Brothers, a Massachusetts-based game manufacturer, but the company rejected his proposal, citing numerous design flaws.

Undeterred, Darrow continued selling handmade copies. Their growing popularity eventually convinced Parker Brothers to reconsider.

In 1935, the company acquired the rights to Darrow’s version and began mass-producing and marketing Monopoly. Parker Brothers also secured rights to earlier related games, including Magie’s original creation.

November 5, 1935: A Landmark in Gaming History
November 5, 1935, is associated with Parker Brothers’ marketing of Monopoly, marking an important milestone in the game’s commercial history.

The timing proved extraordinary. During the Great Depression, millions of Americans faced unemployment, financial insecurity, and the loss of their homes and savings.

Yet Monopoly allowed families to experience an imaginary world of financial opportunity, property ownership, and tremendous wealth.

The game’s combination of strategy, negotiation, luck, and competition made it especially appealing.

By the end of 1935, approximately 250,000 copies had been sold. Sales reportedly exceeded 1.7 million copies in 1936, establishing Monopoly as a nationwide phenomenon.

The Forgotten Inventor
For decades, Charles Darrow was widely credited as Monopoly’s sole inventor.

However, Elizabeth Magie’s earlier contributions were largely overlooked. Parker Brothers had purchased her patent rights for $500, without ongoing royalties.

The game’s commercial success also created a historical irony: an educational tool originally designed to criticize monopolies had become a celebration of acquiring wealth and driving competitors into bankruptcy.

Magie’s role gained greater public recognition decades later, particularly following legal disputes involving the game Anti-Monopoly during the 1970s.

A Worldwide Legacy
Monopoly eventually expanded beyond the United States, becoming an international entertainment phenomenon.

Numerous editions featuring different cities, countries, fictional characters, and popular franchises introduced the game to generations of players.

In 1991, Hasbro acquired Parker Brothers, bringing Monopoly under its ownership.

Today, Monopoly remains one of the world’s best-known board games.

November 5, 2026 / Diary of an Executor

It's been a bit since I've given an update, so let's get you caught up! First up: I close on the house Monday! 

If you've been following along, you know I entertained offers from neighbors before ultimately accepting an investor's offer. Well, while I was on vacation recently, one of the neighbors made a last-ditch offer. He clearly really wanted the house.

Unfortunately, his offer was still significantly less than the investor's, and my job is to act in the best interest of the estate and its beneficiaries. So, onward we go with Monday's closing!

I'm very much looking forward to having that behind me. And, perhaps more importantly, having some actual money to work with!

Next up: The bank accounts!

Here in Indiana, because of how the deceased owned his bank accounts (and because there were no beneficiaries named), the accounts were frozen for 45 days following his death.

Well, we're officially past that 45-day mark, which means I can finally start dealing with those accounts! In fact, I'm heading to the bank today to see what I can accomplish. Will it be a smooth, painless process? Will I walk out with everything handled?

I'm not holding my breath…

All in all, things are moving in the right direction. So much of administering an estate is simply waiting. Waiting on banks. Waiting on paperwork. Waiting on people. Waiting on things that are completely outside your control. And then, seemingly all at once, things start moving!

Fingers crossed that Monday's closing goes smoothly and today's bank adventure doesn't turn into its own not-fun adventure. It is a bank after all…

I'll keep you posted!

Until next time,
Jenny / Executor

Good morning, friends. As the first light of November 5, 2026, gently breaks across the sky at this quiet 5:17 AM hour, I want to share a word of hope drawn from an ancient story that still speaks directly to our hearts today.

The verse for our reflection is from Matthew 1:20: "...do not be afraid to take Mary..." Joseph faced an overwhelming moment. The woman he loved was expecting a child that was not his, and every practical and social reason told him to walk away. Fear of the unknown, fear of judgment, and fear of what the future held must have pressed heavily on him. Yet God sent a messenger with a simple command: do not be afraid.

Many of us wake up carrying similar weights in 2026. Perhaps you are weighing a difficult decision in a relationship, wondering whether to stay and trust when the path ahead feels uncertain. Maybe work pressures, rising costs, or concerns about family health have left you hesitating to take the next step. Across our communities we see people facing division, loneliness, and questions about the future that can make anyone want to pull back and protect themselves.

Still, the angel’s words remind us that God often invites us into situations that require courage we do not yet feel. Joseph’s yes changed history because he chose trust over fear. In the same way, the small acts of faithfulness we offer today—listening to a struggling friend, showing patience at home, or stepping forward in a new opportunity—can open doors we cannot yet see.

Take a moment this morning to breathe and remember you are not alone in whatever uncertainty you carry. God’s plan may look different from what we expect, but it is always rooted in love. Let that truth steady your heart as you move through the day.
