text:
$BKSY Q3 2026 earnings: BlackSky's satellite subscriptions double, and operating cash profit hits record

BlackSky's newer Gen-3 satellites are turning defense trials into high-margin subscriptions while overhead costs barely move. The satellite imagery provider more than doubled revenue to $43 million and reached a 30% Adjusted EBITDA margin. Chief executive Brian E. O'Toole lifted the bottom of the full-year outlook, though by our math the plan has Adjusted EBITDA stepping down to about $9 million in the fourth quarter.

• Revenue: $𝟒𝟐.𝟖𝐌 (+118% from a year ago (+81% adjusted for prior contract cut))
• Space-based intelligence & AI revenue: $𝟑𝟐.𝟕𝐌 (+107% from a year ago, +34% from last quarter)
• Adjusted EBITDA: $𝟏𝟐.𝟖𝐌 (29.8% margin, vs -$4.5M a year ago)
• Full-year revenue outlook: 𝐑𝐚𝐢𝐬𝐞𝐝 𝐟𝐥𝐨𝐨𝐫 $𝟏𝟎𝐌 (now $140–150M (middle of the range: +36% growth))

⚖️ 𝐕𝐞𝐫𝐝𝐢𝐜𝐭: 🟢 Bullish

The story got better because subscription revenue jumped by a third in a single quarter and proved the business can earn 30% cash margins once revenue clears fixed satellite costs. Selection by a French and UAE consortium for 50 satellites also offers an answer to concerns about 2027 sales coverage. Two cautions: reported net income of $19 million came from a non-cash warrant gain rather than operations, and only one satellite launched this quarter against a plan for two.

The question now is whether the consortium deal and recent subscription wins lock in growth for 2027 or leave the company exposed to lumpy government orders and a few foreign buyers. If the new awards are firm, contracted backlog for 2027 will climb well above last quarter's $73 million; if the consortium deal is still an unbooked framework, next year's gap remains. The third-quarter 10-Q backlog and customer concentration tables will tell.

Full article with charts - link in bio

🐂 𝐁𝐮𝐥𝐥 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🟢🟢 𝐒𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐭𝐞 𝐒𝐮𝐛𝐬𝐜𝐫𝐢𝐩𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬 𝐀𝐫𝐞 𝐃𝐫𝐢𝐯𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐇𝐢𝐠𝐡-𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐢𝐧 𝐆𝐫𝐨𝐰𝐭𝐡
BlackSky operates low-earth-orbit satellites and sells their imagery and analytics through two main lines: space-based intelligence subscriptions and custom mission hardware. Subscription demand for its newest Gen-3 satellites is carrying the business, and even after adjusting for last year's $4 million U. S. government contract cut, total revenue grew 81% by our math.

• Space-based intelligence and AI services revenue: $32.7 million, up 107% from a year ago and 34% from last quarter
• Subscription gross margin excluding depreciation: 84.9%, up from 78.0% last quarter by our math
• Advanced technology programs (customer-funded research): $5.4 million, up 81% from a year ago
• Mission solutions (satellite hardware builds): $4.7 million, compared with $0.9 million a year ago

Trial contracts are turning into recurring revenue across defense and space customers. An international defense client expanded a small trial "into a seven-figure Gen-3 Assured subscription contract in less than six months", while the satellite group also completed "a 2-month seven-figure assured Gen-3 pilot with the U. S. government" and renewed its space-monitoring deal with HEO.

What to watch: fourth-quarter subscription revenue when full-year results arrive. Another sequential increase above $32.7 million would prove that the third-quarter jump came from recurring contracts rather than one-time delivery milestones.

🟢🟢 𝐅𝐥𝐚𝐭 𝐎𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐡𝐞𝐚𝐝 𝐂𝐨𝐬𝐭𝐬 𝐏𝐮𝐬𝐡𝐞𝐝 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐟𝐢𝐭 𝐭𝐨 𝐚 𝐑𝐞𝐜𝐨𝐫𝐝
"Building on strong Gen-3 sales performance, we delivered an exceptional third quarter with record revenue, strong margin growth, and record adjusted EBITDA," chief executive Brian E. O'Toole said. Because operating a satellite network costs roughly the same whether one customer or ten buy the imagery, new subscription sales flow almost directly into profit.

The numbers confirm O'Toole's claim. Revenue rose $23.2 million from a year ago, but the cost of sales — the direct expense of delivering imagery and hardware, excluding depreciation — rose only $2.3 million, dropping from 35% of revenue to 21%. Selling, general and administrative overhead fell by 51.5 percentage points of revenue, to 59.3%, by our math.

Keeping cash overhead near $21.4 million allowed the Virginia-based company to generate $405 thousand in GAAP operating income, its first operating profit in the past two years. Adjusted EBITDA — operating cash profit before stock compensation, depreciation and warrant swings — reached $12.8 million, or 29.8% of sales.

What to watch: fourth-quarter Adjusted EBITDA margin against the 17.9% implied by the middle of the full-year outlook. Holding above 25% would show that management's fourth-quarter plan is cautious.

🟢 𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐬𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐢𝐮𝐦 𝐏𝐢𝐜𝐤𝐬 𝐁𝐥𝐚𝐜𝐤𝐒𝐤𝐲 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝟓𝟎 𝐒𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐭𝐞𝐬
Foreign governments increasingly want their own dedicated reconnaissance satellites rather than just buying photos from U. S. operators. BlackSky was named the "exclusive provider of very-high resolution optical satellites under a $1 billion investment through a consortium that includes France and the UAE for an initial constellation of 50 satellites" to serve European and other markets.

A 50-satellite order dwarfs the company's own commercial fleet and validates its decision to buy satellite manufacturer LeoStella in 2024. However, the press release does not say how much of the $1 billion consortium budget comes to the satellite maker, when firm contracts will be signed, or when hardware deliveries begin.

What to watch: contracted backlog in the third-quarter filing. A jump of several hundred million dollars above last quarter's $378 million would show the 50-satellite selection is already a binding contract rather than an unbooked framework agreement.

🐻 𝐁𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🔴🔴 𝐑𝐞𝐩𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐟𝐢𝐭 𝐑𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐬 𝐨𝐧 𝐖𝐚𝐫𝐫𝐚𝐧𝐭 𝐀𝐜𝐜𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐃𝐢𝐥𝐮𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧
BlackSky highlighted $18.5 million in third-quarter net income at the top of its release. That headline profit did not come from satellite operations. It came from a $19.7 million non-cash accounting gain on derivative liabilities — equity warrants whose accounting value falls when the stock moves, creating paper income.

• GAAP net income: $18.5 million, compared with a $15.3 million net loss a year ago
• Pre-tax loss excluding the $19.7 million warrant gain: $1.2 million by our math
• Diluted share count: 43.3 million, up 23.0% from 35.2 million a year ago
• Nine-month stock sales: $160.0 million in net cash raised by issuing new shares

Without the warrant adjustment, the company lost $1.2 million before taxes because $3.6 million in interest expense outweighed its $405 thousand operating profit. Meanwhile, the share sales that funded the balance sheet expanded the diluted share count by nearly a quarter, reducing each existing share's claim on future earnings.

What to watch: financing cash inflows in the fourth-quarter report. Further share sales while sitting on $231 million in cash would mean dilution continues despite positive operating cash flow.

🔴 𝐎𝐧𝐥𝐲 𝐎𝐧𝐞 𝐒𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐭𝐞 𝐋𝐚𝐮𝐧𝐜𝐡𝐞𝐝 𝐀𝐠𝐚𝐢𝐧𝐬𝐭 𝐚 𝐓𝐰𝐨-𝐒𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐭𝐞 𝐏𝐥𝐚𝐧
Gen-3 satellites are the spacecraft that produce BlackSky's sharpest 35-centimeter imagery. Entering the quarter, four Gen-3 units were in orbit, and management planned to launch two more during the third quarter on the way to eight satellites in space by the end of 2026.

During the quarter, the operator deployed only its "fifth Gen-3 satellite, achieving first light and revenue generating operations within 24 hours". Getting the spacecraft into commercial service in a single day proves the hardware works smoothly, but launching one unit instead of two extends a pattern of delayed deployment targets.

What to watch: the number of Gen-3 satellites launched in the fourth quarter. Reaching the year-end target of eight now requires three launches in three months, and falling short would limit imaging capacity for new regions in 2027.

🔴 𝐑𝐢𝐬𝐤𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐪𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐝𝐢𝐝𝐧'𝐭 𝐚𝐧𝐬𝐰𝐞𝐫
Four standing concerns from prior quarters cannot be read from the earnings release and await the quarterly Form 10-Q filing.

• Backlog scheduled for 2027: stood at just $72.6 million last quarter, well below 2026 sales; the filing's backlog footnote will show whether new awards filled the 2027 gap.
• Customer concentration: two foreign governments accounted for 33% of revenue last quarter and one client held 44% of receivables; the concentration footnote will show if the third-quarter jump relied on the same two buyers.
• U. S. government Electro-Optical Commercial Layer (EOCL) contract: the release notes a completed two-month U. S. government pilot, but the geographic table will show whether overall U. S. sales stopped shrinking.
• Contract accounting catch-ups: mission solutions gained $1.8 million from favorable cost-estimate revisions last quarter; the accounting footnote will show if similar one-time adjustments aided third-quarter profit.

👓 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐓𝐡𝐞𝐦𝐞𝐬

𝐆𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐧𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐁𝐮𝐝𝐠𝐞𝐭 𝐂𝐚𝐮𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐑𝐞𝐦𝐚𝐢𝐧𝐬 𝐢𝐧 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐎𝐮𝐭𝐥𝐨𝐨𝐤
Defense agencies in the United States and abroad supply almost all of BlackSky's revenue. In its outlook commentary, the company continued to flag "long and unpredictable sales cycles, customer demand, U. S. government budget uncertainties" as primary factors that can delay when signed government contracts turn into recognized sales.

— • — • —

💲 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐊𝐏𝐈𝐬

𝐅𝐫𝐞𝐞 𝐜𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐟𝐥𝐨𝐰 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): -$𝟏𝟏.𝟖 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇄ reversing
Cash burn narrowed by our math from -$18.9 million in the second quarter as operating cash flow turned positive at $3.6 million. Subtracting $15.4 million of capital spending on satellites and ground equipment left free cash flow at -$11.8 million, compared with -$54.0 million in the third quarter of 2025.

𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐢𝐧𝐯𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐬 𝐯𝐬 𝐭𝐨𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐝𝐞𝐛𝐭 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟐𝟑𝟏.𝟏 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐜𝐚𝐬𝐡 / $𝟐𝟏𝟗.𝟗 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐝𝐞𝐛𝐭  ⇒ stable
Total cash, restricted cash and short-term investments fell by $13.0 million from the second quarter's $244.1 million, matching the quarter's satellite capital spending. With $219.9 million in current and long-term debt on the balance sheet, the satellite operator holds $11.3 million in net cash by our math.

𝐂𝐮𝐫𝐫𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐜𝐭 𝐥𝐢𝐚𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐞𝐬 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟏𝟕.𝟕 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
Current contract liabilities — cash customers have paid upfront for services to be delivered within a year — declined for a third straight quarter. The balance dropped 13.6% by our math from $20.5 million at the end of 2025 as the group recognizes revenue from earlier prepayments faster than new upfront cash arrives.

— • — • —

🔮 𝐆𝐮𝐢𝐝𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟔 𝐑𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞: $𝟏𝟒𝟎–𝟏𝟓𝟎 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
🠅 raised from $130–150 million
Raised. Management lifted the bottom of the range by $10 million while keeping the top unchanged, putting the middle of the plan at $145 million, or 36.1% annual growth by our math. That leaves $48.1 million for the fourth quarter (+36.5% from a year ago against a tougher hardware comparison). Across four quarters, the middle of the plan moved +$7.5M, $0M, and +$5.0M.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟔 𝐀𝐝𝐣𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐄𝐁𝐈𝐓𝐃𝐀: $𝟏𝟖–𝟐𝟒 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
🠅 raised from $12–24 million
Raised. The company lifted the floor by $6 million and kept the ceiling at $24 million, moving the middle of the range up $3 million to $21 million. By our math, subtracting $12.4 million earned in the first nine months leaves $8.6 million for the fourth quarter — down from $12.8 million in the third quarter. Earlier raises moved the middle by +$6.0M, $0M, and +$3.0M.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟔 𝐂𝐚𝐩𝐢𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐞𝐱𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐞𝐬: $𝟓𝟎–𝟔𝟎 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
🠆 unchanged from $50–60 million
Unchanged. The satellite builder kept its full-year spending plan at a $55 million middle for a third straight quarter. Because property purchases and satellite construction totaled $46.5 million across the first nine months, the plan leaves about $8.5 million in capital spending for the fourth quarter by our math, down from $15.4 million in the third quarter.

— • — • —

❓ 𝐊𝐞𝐲 𝐐𝐮𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬

𝐇𝐨𝐰 𝐝𝐨𝐞𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞 $𝟏 𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐬𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐢𝐮𝐦 𝐝𝐞𝐚𝐥 𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐛𝐚𝐜𝐤𝐥𝐨𝐠?
BlackSky was named the exclusive provider for 50 satellites under a $1 billion consortium investment with France and the UAE. Investors need to know BlackSky's dollar share, whether the contract is binding yet, and how much revenue it adds to 2027.

𝐖𝐡𝐲 𝐝𝐨𝐞𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐨𝐮𝐭𝐥𝐨𝐨𝐤 𝐢𝐦𝐩𝐥𝐲 𝐥𝐨𝐰𝐞𝐫 𝐟𝐨𝐮𝐫𝐭𝐡-𝐪𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐟𝐢𝐭?
By our math, the full-year plan implies fourth-quarter revenue rising to $48.1 million while Adjusted EBITDA drops from $12.8 million to $8.6 million. Management did not explain whether lower-margin hardware deliveries or higher overhead cause that drop.

𝐀𝐫𝐞 𝐞𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐭 𝐆𝐞𝐧-𝟑 𝐬𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐭𝐞𝐬 𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐞𝐱𝐩𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐛𝐲 𝐲𝐞𝐚𝐫-𝐞𝐧𝐝?
Only one Gen-3 satellite launched in the third quarter against a prior plan for two, bringing the fleet to five. Hitting the year-end target of eight would require launching three satellites in the fourth quarter.

𝐇𝐨𝐰 𝐦𝐮𝐜𝐡 𝐝𝐢𝐝 𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐜𝐭 𝐜𝐚𝐭𝐜𝐡-𝐮𝐩𝐬 𝐨𝐫 𝐭𝐰𝐨 𝐛𝐮𝐲𝐞𝐫𝐬 𝐝𝐫𝐢𝐯𝐞 𝐬𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬?
Last quarter relied on two foreign governments for a third of revenue and gained $1.8 million from contract accounting revisions. Because the release omits both figures, the 10-Q filing must show how concentrated the $32.7 million subscription quarter was.

text:
The first primary school I went to was a C of E (Church of England) school. C of E schools are state funded, secular, and free to attend. Despite being secular, they are open to children of any background including religion, and are meant to retain a Christian characteristic. The one I attended certainly had a Christian characteristic. It was called Christ Church School, and was in St Leonards-on-Sea, Hastings. It had a large gothic church (which is still there) called Christ Church next to it. Assemblies were held in the church, where hymns were sung, and the Lord's Prayer was recited. The school itself moved to newly built premises fairly nearby, after either my first or second year at the school. My brother, who's around two years my senior, wanted to move schools, so I moved with him to the final primary school I attended, which was West St Leonards School in Hastings. This school was likely a C of E school as well, as there were morning assemblies in which hymns were sung, and although I have no clear recollection, the Lord's Prayer was likely recited on occasion. This school had a large recreational field attached to it, and two fairly large playgrounds. The secondary school (which in the US and other places is called a high school) I attended was a state school (which is free to attend and open to those within the catchment area). Fee paying private schools in the UK are also referred to as public schools, the linguistic reasoning behind this was because they were open to children from any locality. In the US, Canada, Australia and other places, a public school refers to a free to attend state funded school. The secondary school I went to was called the Grove School, and it was for all intents and purposes a fairly rough school. 
Neither of my parents are religious, but are spiritual sentient beings nonetheless. This is as true today as it was then.
As a child and as an adult, I would visit my maternal grandparents in Hove, East Sussex. Hove was then a town, but is now part of Brighton & Hove City. I remember my grandmother with fondness, especially of the times when I would visit her as a child. I remember my grandfather as being a fairly grumpy distant man, but I understand that he was someone who was ultimately able to provide for his family. They ran a successful business together, which I think mostly involved sourcing furniture for restaurants in the Brighton & Hove area. Their names were Jack and Norma Waring. Norma died aged 90 in 2016, and to the best of my recollection, Jack died around ten years earlier at the age of 88. I don't think they would have described themselves as religious, but from time to time, both Jack and Norma attended Brighton & Hove Reform synagogue, and later Brighton & Hove Progressive Synagogue. Neither of them were particularly political, and their attendance at either synagogue would have been for the community value that was offered. As a pre-adolescent child I went once with my grandmother to the Reform synagogue, and it was during Hanukkah, which was something I had not heard of before. I remember there was food, some other children there, and a talk by the Rabbi that included the story attached to the festival. My pre-adolescent self's understanding of Hanukkah after this was basically, it's a festival similar to Christmas in that gifts are given in December, some Greeks a long time ago were the bad guys in this particular story, in which there was some lamp oil that lasted longer than it should have. 
My grandparents and extended family celebrated Christmas, and with my parents and siblings, I would often spend time with them over this period.

text:
4.1 Million Solar Systems, Paid by the Month: How Light Reached 20 Million People

In early 2003, electricity access reached only 27 percent of the rural population in Bangladesh, according to the World Bank (@WorldBankGroup). That year a state-owned development finance company called IDCOL began a pilot to sell solar home systems to 50,000 households. The pilot's target was reached within three years. By 2018 the program had sold more than 4.1 million systems, giving about 20 million people electricity, which the World Bank's 2021 book on the program puts at about 14 percent of the country's population.

This case opens the second season of The Constraint Tax because it answers a question founders in Kampala ask me often: what do you do about power while the larger system keeps building out? Season one measured what unreliable power costs a business. Season two follows constraints that were solved, how long it took, who paid, and what a founder can do inside the constraint today.

𝗛𝗼𝘄 𝗶𝗻𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗹𝗹𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀 𝗽𝘂𝘁 𝗮 𝘀𝗼𝗹𝗮𝗿 𝗽𝗮𝗻𝗲𝗹 𝗼𝗻 𝗮 𝗿𝗼𝗼𝗳

A solar home system is a panel, a battery, a charge controller and a few lights, with a socket for a phone charger. Its problem was never the technology. It was the price paid in one go by a household that earns money in small amounts, week by week.

IDCOL's answer was to let the households pay in small amounts too. According to the World Bank's book Living in the Light (Cabraal, Ward, Bogach and Jain, 2021), IDCOL did not sell the systems itself. It recruited partner organizations, mainly NGOs and microfinance lenders, five in 2003 and 57 by 2015. The partners sold systems on credit, with payments spread over up to three years at interest rates of 12 to 16 percent, and a down payment typically of 15 percent. The partners selected customers, extended the loan, installed the system and provided after-sale service. IDCOL lent to the partners at 6 percent over ten years and paid a small grant on each system, which fell from 19 percent of the cost in 2003 to 5 percent by 2017. Technical inspectors checked installations before grants were paid.

The arithmetic that made it work sat in the household's existing spending. Samad, Khandker, Asaduzzaman and Yunus (World Bank, 2013) compared adopters with non-adopters using a household survey from 2012. Households with a solar home system used under one liter of kerosene a month, against almost three liters for households without one, and the authors put the saving at 160 taka a month. The book describes the logic: the savings from not buying kerosene and not paying to recharge batteries could go toward the monthly repayment.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝘆𝗲𝗮𝗿𝘀 𝗶𝘁 𝘁𝗼𝗼𝗸, 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘄𝗵𝗼 𝗽𝗮𝗶𝗱

The program started with a 50,000-household pilot, and its installed base rose to 236,000 by 2009. It reached 1.88 million by December 2012. Sales peaked at 816,000 in 2013, when about 16 percent of the rural population was getting electricity through solar home systems. The program's goal was passed by June 2016, and the 4.1 million total was reached in 2018. Spread across 15 years, that averages about 273,000 systems a year (my arithmetic).

The bill was shared. The World Bank estimates the total investment at US$1,095 million, about US$266 per household. Grants of US$80.9 million came from the Global Environment Facility and other donors, which is about 7.4 percent of the total (my arithmetic). Households' own down payments came to US$160 million. The rest was credit from the World Bank, the Asian Development Bank and others, which the partner organizations repaid out of the monthly installments.

The record is also candid about what went less well. Partner collection efficiency was 94 percent or better through 2009, then fell to 52 percent in 2016 and 38 percent in 2017. The book attributes the change mainly to the rapidly expanding grid, which gave households another source of electricity. A pay-as-you-go meter retrofit tried from 2015 to 2017 did not work, because the market in Bangladesh was too small for the product cost. The program closed its installations in 2018, and the World Bank says it then supported solar irrigation, mini-grids and rooftop solar.

The households wanted electricity. Many got it first from a panel, and then the grid reached them.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗸𝗲𝗿: 𝗖.𝗞. 𝗣𝗿𝗮𝗵𝗮𝗹𝗮𝗱, 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘂𝗻𝗶𝘁 𝘀𝗶𝘇𝗲𝗱 𝘁𝗼 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗽𝗼𝗰𝗸𝗲𝘁

C.K. Prahalad's The Fortune at the Bottom of the Pyramid (2004) gave this approach its business argument. He wrote that the way to reach customers with small and uneven cash flows is "to make unit packages that are small and, therefore, affordable." His reason: "The poor have unpredictable income streams. Many subsist on daily wages and have to use cash conservatively. They tend to make purchases only when they have cash and buy only what they need for that day."

His "Three As" are affordability, access and availability. He gives affordability as "whether it is a single-serve package or novel purchasing schemes, the key is affordability without sacrificing quality or efficacy." The word "installment" does not appear in the chapter pages I could open, so I will not claim he proposed it. What he proposed is the principle behind it: price the product to the customer's cash flow.

Bangladesh applied that principle to a capital good. The unit of purchase went from a lump sum to a monthly amount, and the seller stayed in charge of installation and service, which households cannot do for themselves.

𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗨𝗴𝗮𝗻𝗱𝗮 𝗵𝗮𝘀 𝗮𝗹𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗱𝘆 𝗱𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝘄𝗲𝗹𝗹

Uganda's own numbers show the same two paths running side by side. The Uganda Bureau of Statistics' (@StatisticsUg) National Population and Housing Census 2024 (Final Report, Volume 1) found that 53.4 percent of households have access to electricity. Of Uganda's 10,698,913 households, 3,006,732, or 28.1 percent, use solar as their main source of lighting, including 33.3 percent of rural households. Grid and mini-grid electricity was the main lighting source for 25.3 percent.

Generation has grown as well. A 2025 article from the Ministry of Finance's (@mofpedU) Development Policy and Performance Portal, citing the Electricity Regulatory Authority, reports installed generation capacity of about 2,048 MW in 2024, up 63.7 percent from 1,251 MW in 2020, largely from the Isimba (183 MW) and Karuma (600 MW) dams.

There is a private market too. The Efficiency for Access Coalition's Uganda country profile reports that off-grid solar lighting sales by GOGLA affiliates rose 9 percent from 368,000 units in 2018 to 400,000 in 2019. Companies including Ignite Energy Access and Sun King list Uganda among their markets, and the profile notes that pay-as-you-go financing is a key enabler for the Ugandan market.

Three million Ugandan households have already made the choice a founder is facing.

𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗮 𝗳𝗼𝘂𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗿 𝗰𝗮𝗻 𝗱𝗼 𝗶𝗻𝘀𝗶𝗱𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘀𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗶𝗻𝘁 𝘁𝗼𝗱𝗮𝘆

These suggestions are mine. They draw on the evidence above, and I mark the arithmetic that is only illustrative.

Start by measuring. For 30 days, write down every outage in hours and, if you run a generator, the liters of fuel it burned. Multiply the liters by the price you paid, then add the sales you lost in those hours. That number is the monthly cost of the constraint for your business, and it is the figure any solar quote has to beat.

Size the critical load. List the devices that must keep running when the grid is off, with their watts and the hours you need them. A laptop at 60 W, a router at 12 W and three LED bulbs at 5 W each come to 87 W; six hours of that is about 522 watt-hours. That is illustrative arithmetic, and an installer will adjust it for losses and battery limits, but it turns "we need backup" into a number you can ask three suppliers to quote.

Ask every supplier for the payback in months. A randomized trial in rural Kenya (Rom, Pomeranz and Günther, 2025; 1,286 households) found that basic solar lights, priced at US$9, paid back their cost in expenditure savings after 9 months, and a larger light at US$24 after 19 months, and that kerosene use fell by half. Your payback depends on your fuel spend, but you can ask for it in the same form.

If you sell products or services that depend on power, learn from the Bangladesh structure. Offer tiers. Ask for a small down payment, around 10 to 15 percent as in the program, and spread the rest over months. Keep the seller in charge of installation and service. Verify that the work was done before you pay out in full, which is what IDCOL's inspectors did.

Use the census split to pick where to sell. Solar is the main lighting source for 33.3 percent of rural households and 20.6 percent of urban ones in the UBOS tables.

Work with installers who stay for the service. Ignite Energy Access and Sun King both describe pay-as-you-go or EasyBuy offers in Uganda. I could confirm Sun King only as a rendered page, and I have no default or repayment figures for either in Uganda, so ask for references from customers who have paid for two years.

Each of these needs one month of notes and three quotes.

𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗜 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗸, 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘄𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗜 𝘄𝗼𝘂𝗹𝗱 𝗱𝗼

Power can feel like weather to a founder, something that happens to the business. The Bangladesh program treated it as a purchase with a monthly price. That is the framing I would borrow first, because a monthly price can be compared, negotiated and planned around, and weather cannot.

If I were running a small business here this month, I would do three things. Measure 30 days of outages and fuel before talking to any supplier. Get three written quotes for the same critical load, each showing payback in months. Then put power in the plan as a line item, decided once a quarter, the way I would decide rent.

One idea I would back: a shared system for a street or market of small shops. One installer sizes a single battery and panel set for the group, each shop pays by the month for its share, and the installer stays responsible for service. It borrows the partner-organization structure from the Bangladesh program, and a few shops and a month of logged data would be enough to test it.

Papal AI Ethics and State Power: The Limits of Global Enforcement 
- Principal assessment — High confidence: The five propositions establish a coherent ethical framework but do not themselves create international legal obligations. Their strategic weight lies in their ability to influence future treaty language, domestic regulatory standards, defence-procurement rules and institutional accountability.

The central conflict — High confidence: The requirement that humans retain effective authority over decisions affecting life and liberty is compatible with existing obligations to comply with international humanitarian law. A comprehensive prohibition on lethal autonomous weapons, however, goes beyond currently established international restrictions and conflicts with the military value attributed to autonomous capabilities.

The negotiating reality — High confidence: The United Nations General Assembly’s December 2025 resolution urged progress toward an instrument on lethal autonomous weapons. The Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons process remained directed toward negotiating elements of an instrument without prejudging whether it would be legally binding. mandates.

Institutional asymmetry — High confidence: International scientific assessment and political dialogue have developed faster than international inspection, enforcement and remedies mechanisms. Scientific coordination cannot substitute for compulsory jurisdiction or national implementation.

Corporate exposure — Medium-high confidence: Stronger human-accountability requirements could increase spending on system evaluation, traceability, operational safeguards and legal documentation. Their eventual distribution across developers, deployers, manufacturers and public authorities will depend on jurisdiction-specific rules.

Competitive asymmetry — High confidence: States and firms controlling advanced computing infrastructure, semiconductor supply chains, critical software and proprietary model capabilities have greater practical influence over access conditions than institutions whose authority is principally advisory.

Distributional concern — Medium confidence: Common-good commitments will have limited distributive effect without financing, accessible computing infrastructure, technical capacity-building and mechanisms that allow less-resourced countries to participate in governance rather than merely adopt externally defined standards.

2030 outlook — Medium confidence: Selective institutionalisation of transparency, lifecycle assurance and human-control requirements is a plausible pathway. A comprehensive, globally verifiable prohibition on lethal autonomous weapons would require substantially greater agreement on definitions, military exemptions, inspection rights and enforcement than the current record establishes.

Decision consequence: Governments should distinguish three different objectives: improving accountability under existing law, negotiating additional restrictions on autonomous weapons, and building international institutions capable of monitoring compliance. These objectives have different legal authorities, implementation costs and diplomatic prospects.

Decisive uncertainty: Whether the principal military and technological powers will accept restrictions that reduce unilateral operational flexibility, expose sensitive capabilities to external scrutiny or limit their ability to exploit advances in autonomous targeting.

Papal AI Ethics and State Power: Who Will Enforce the Limits of Artificial Intelligence?
The decisive question raised by Pope Leo XIV is not whether artificial intelligence should remain under human authority, but whether governments will accept enforceable restrictions when autonomy delivers military advantages, industrial power and geopolitical leverage. His five propositions of 30 October 2026 reject machine personhood, prohibit the delegation of decisions affecting life and liberty, demand equitable technological benefits and call for effective international institutions. Yet the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons has not produced a binding prohibition on lethal autonomous weapons. The European Union regulates high-risk civilian AI while excluding relevant military and national-security activities. Meanwhile, governments are investing billions in computing infrastructure and competing for control over advanced semiconductors. The contradiction is immediate: ethical agreement is expanding precisely as the economic and security incentives to preserve technological discretion become stronger.

Fifty Governments Want Negotiations. None Has Yet Secured a Global Ban.
The diplomatic record is more substantial than the conventional opposition between ethical ambition and governmental indifference suggests. On 4 September 2026, the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons Group of Governmental Experts adopted by consensus a report containing elements for a possible international instrument on lethal autonomous weapons. Its provisions address target identification, selection and engagement without human intervention, responsible chains of command, operational restrictions, testing and accountability. On 22 October 2026, a coalition of 50 states, including Italy, France and Germany, welcomed those elements and called for a negotiating mandate. The International Committee of the Red Cross separately reported that more than 70 states supported beginning negotiations. These figures establish political momentum, not agreement on a binding prohibition. The distinction will be tested at the CCW’s Seventh Review Conference in Geneva on 16–20 November 2026. CCW Final Report, CCW/GGE.1/2026/3 — United Nations Office for Disarmament Affairs — September 2026.

The disagreement concerns the precise point at which machine execution becomes an unacceptable delegation of human judgment. The United States Department of Defense’s Directive 3000.09, reissued on 25 January 2023, regulates autonomous and semi-autonomous weapons through requirements concerning appropriate human judgment, testing and oversight rather than prohibiting every autonomous function. The United Kingdom accepts context-dependent human involvement, including parameters established before operation. France rejects systems falling within its nationally defined category of fully autonomous lethal weapons. Germany distinguishes constrained rapid defensive responses from autonomous operations in more complex environments. All can endorse human responsibility while maintaining different operational doctrines. A treaty that leaves these distinctions unresolved risks either restricting capabilities governments regard as indispensable or defining prohibited autonomy so narrowly that existing programmes remain largely unaffected.

International humanitarian law already requires distinction, proportionality and feasible precautions in attack. Article 36 of Additional Protocol I also requires its High Contracting Parties to review new weapons for compatibility with applicable international law. But an obligation to conduct a legal review is not equivalent to a prohibition on autonomous engagement. Nor does successful technical testing demonstrate that a system can lawfully operate in every environment. The central treaty question is whether certain autonomous functions must be prohibited independently of national assessments of military necessity. Additional Protocol I, Article 36 — International Committee of the Red Cross — June 1977.

The Military Advantage Lies Precisely Where Human Control Becomes Hardest
Autonomous engagement becomes militarily attractive when communication is disrupted, threats arrive rapidly or several platforms must operate simultaneously. A human commander may define an operating area, identify authorised target categories and approve activation, while the system subsequently selects and engages objects without a separate command for every action. That arrangement is fundamentally different from allowing software to determine independently whether an individual should be killed. Yet the legal distinction becomes difficult when target characteristics, operating conditions and the consequences of engagement change after activation.

The September 2026 CCW consensus report recognises direct and indirect human control, while addressing operational limits on geography, duration, target categories and scale. This reflects the operational problem rather than resolving it. A human authorisation recorded before activation may be legally significant, but it cannot automatically validate every subsequent engagement. Conversely, requiring a separate human command for every defensive response could impose limitations that some governments consider incompatible with the speed of the threat. The central requirement is therefore not the ceremonial presence of an operator but demonstrable authority over the weapon’s permitted behaviour.

Verification compounds the disagreement. Autonomous functionality may depend on software configuration, sensor inputs and operating parameters rather than on easily identifiable physical characteristics. A system inspected in one configuration may subsequently be updated. A successful test in a controlled environment does not prove compliance under different conditions. Inspectors might require access to source code, operational records or classified targeting information that governments and defence contractors are reluctant to disclose. Without credible arrangements for examining those functions, even a formally binding prohibition could leave compliance dependent heavily on national declarations.

The Real Enforcement Deficit Is Institutional, Not Philosophical
On 26 August 2025, the United Nations General Assembly established the Independent International Scientific Panel on Artificial Intelligence, comprising 40 members, and the Global Dialogue on AI Governance. The Dialogue’s inaugural meeting in Geneva on 6–7 July 2026 brought delegations from 163 countries. Its next meeting is scheduled for 3–4 May 2027 in New York. These institutions broaden scientific assessment and political participation, particularly for governments lacking extensive domestic expertise. They do not possess general authority to inspect military systems, compel proprietary disclosures or impose sanctions. Participation by 163 countries therefore measures diplomatic reach, not regulatory jurisdiction. UN General Assembly Resolution A/RES/79/325 — United Nations — August 2025.

The European Union offers a different model because Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, the Artificial Intelligence Act, imposes enforceable obligations within its legal scope. Yet the AI Omnibus, effective 27 July 2026, revised the timetable: relevant Annex III high-risk requirements now apply from 2 December 2027, with corresponding Annex I product requirements following on 2 August 2028. The amendments reflect the collision between regulatory ambition and implementation capacity. Documentation, testing and human oversight require technical expertise and investment; smaller suppliers cannot necessarily absorb those costs as easily as established technology groups. The regulation also excludes relevant military, defence and national-security activities, leaving the most consequential autonomous-weapons questions to separate legal and diplomatic processes. AI Omnibus Enters into Force — European Commission — July 2026.

The Council of Europe’s Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law, opened for signature on 5 September 2024, supplies a further treaty pathway. The European Union deposited its instrument of approval on 15 May 2026. But treaty commitments, domestic enforcement and international inspection remain distinct. The Convention’s entry-into-force conditions and national implementation requirements cannot be replaced by political endorsement. The institutional deficit is therefore specific: the international system can formulate principles and negotiate obligations more readily than it can establish compulsory access to the evidence needed to investigate violations.

Computing Power Has Become an Instrument of Foreign Policy
The economic contest surrounding AI is governed by infrastructure that ethical declarations cannot redistribute. The International Energy Agency estimated global data-centre electricity consumption at approximately 485 terawatt-hours in 2025 and projected approximately 950 TWh annually by 2030 under its updated central scenario. The difference, approximately 465 TWh, is additional projected annual electricity consumption, not generating capacity already commissioned. These figures cover data centres generally, not exclusively AI. They nevertheless expose the physical constraint on technological expansion: computing ambitions require electricity, grid connections, specialised equipment and finance. Key Questions on Energy and AI — International Energy Agency — 2026.

The industrial consequences are equally direct. In January 2026, the US Bureau of Industry and Security revised licensing treatment for specified advanced semiconductors exported to China, including the NVIDIA H200 and AMD MI325X, allowing case-by-case consideration subject to security conditions. Control over advanced chips therefore translates into influence over foreign computing programmes, investment decisions and supply relationships. Access to AI services does not confer control over the infrastructure or intellectual property required to develop them independently. A government can endorse equitable technological benefits while restricting strategically sensitive inputs; the resulting distribution of capability is determined by licensing, capital and productive capacity, not by the universality of the ethical language.

The divide begins below frontier computing. The International Telecommunication Union estimated that 2.2 billion people remained offline in 2025. Internet use reached 94% in high-income countries, against 23% in low-income countries. These figures measure connectivity, not advanced AI capability, but they demonstrate why access cannot be reduced to the commercial availability of models. Countries lacking reliable networks, technical expertise and computing resources cannot exercise the same practical control over AI development as those possessing the infrastructure. Common-good commitments acquire economic meaning only when financing and capacity-building produce operational capabilities rather than additional declarations. Measuring Digital Development: Facts and Figures 2025 — International Telecommunication Union — November 2025.

Europe Can Regulate AI More Quickly Than It Can Build Independence
Europe’s national programmes demonstrate the distance between regulatory authority and productive capacity. Italy established differentiated responsibilities for the National Cybersecurity Agency, ACN, and the Agency for Digital Italy, AgID, through its 2025 AI legislation, alongside a €1 billion programme supporting startups and SMEs in AI and related technologies. The IT4LIA AI Factory secured an infrastructure procurement contract in April 2026, strengthening the computing ecosystem associated with CINECA and Bologna. The programme creates capacity for industrial research and development, but a procurement contract is not proof of completed deployment or measurable productivity growth. IT4LIA AI Factory Procurement — EuroHPC Joint Undertaking — April 2026.

France announced €109 billion in prospective AI-related investment in February 2025, with particular emphasis on computing infrastructure and the attraction of data-centre projects. Germany’s Hightech Agenda Deutschland pursues a different industrial transmission mechanism: by 2030, it targets AI-based activity representing 10% of German economic output, a fourfold increase in AI startups relative to 2025 and AI adoption by more than 50% of manufacturing SMEs by 2029. The French figure concerns prospective investment, while Germany’s figures are policy targets rather than achieved output or independently estimated GDP gains. Their difference matters because large computing installations and industrial deployment generate economic value through distinct channels.

Outside the EU regulatory framework, the United Kingdom’s 2025 Compute Roadmap envisages up to £2 billion for public computing and expansion of its AI Research Resource from 21 AI ExaFLOPS in 2025 to 420 by 2030, using the government’s stated performance measure. At EU level, the Commission reports 19 AI Factories and 13 associated antennas being established, while the Chips Act is associated with expectations of more than €43 billion in public investment and over €100 billion in broader policy-driven public and private semiconductor investment through 2030. These envelopes must not be added together as completed expenditure. They reveal a common constraint: European governments are attempting to enlarge their technological capacity while remaining exposed to international semiconductor supply chains, infrastructure-delivery schedules and competition for capital. UK Compute Roadmap — UK Department for Science, Innovation and Technology — July 2025; European Chips Act — European Commission.

The Next Twenty-Four Months Will Separate Governance from Declaration
Between November 2026 and November 2028, the institutional test will become measurable. The CCW Review Conference must determine whether the September consensus elements become the basis for substantive negotiations. The UN Global Dialogue will reconvene in May 2027, while the EU’s revised high-risk AI requirements take effect across relevant categories in December 2027 and August 2028. None of these milestones automatically establishes effective compliance. The decisive evidence will be binding language, national implementing measures, technical assurance procedures, actual regulatory enforcement and credible access to information when violations are alleged.

The financial consequences will fall unevenly. Defence ministries that cannot establish reliable human-control and testing procedures will face procurement uncertainty, operational risk and potentially expensive modifications. AI suppliers will bear documentation, evaluation and contractual compliance costs, with smaller firms less able to spread fixed expenditure across large product portfolios. European governments that fail to convert computing commitments into functioning facilities will continue paying for technological dependence through external infrastructure, software and specialised components. Countries lacking independent assessment capacity will remain dependent on suppliers not only for technology but also for the evidence needed to evaluate it.

The choice now confronting governments is therefore concrete. The five propositions of 30 October 2026 can remain a standard against which conduct is publicly judged, become the foundation for national assurance obligations, or contribute to binding restrictions on particular autonomous-weapons functions. Each outcome carries different costs and grants different degrees of discretion. Inaction will not preserve the existing balance: military and corporate programmes will continue under their applicable legal regimes, while compliance burdens, infrastructure investment and technological dependencies evolve. The governments and firms that finance the infrastructure will shape the available capabilities; those that neglect implementation will inherit the costs of dependence, weak oversight and legal uncertainty. -

Mark, you call Tucker the spiritual leader of his followers. Look at your own record before you hand out that title.

In 2018 you said no tariffs and no subsidies was the Levin position. You called Trump's steel tariffs a tax on Americans and a favor for the connected. In 2025 the same policy became a growth plan. The economics did not change. The man imposing it did. Why does Trump get a pass from you?

Tariffs are a tax paid by Americans. The Tax Foundation, the free market think tank conservatives have cited for decades, found they cost the average household $1,000 last year, the largest tax increase as a share of GDP since 1993. Add trillions in deficit spending and inflation climbed back to 3.4 percent by August. Voters felt it at the register, and 89 percent of them said cost of living drove their vote. You warned about exactly this for years. Where was that Mark Levin this year?

You warn about the debt. Trump added $7.8 trillion in his first term and another $3.7 trillion so far in this one, roughly $11.5 trillion, and the total crossed $40 trillion in August with no plan to reverse it. COVID is no excuse. Trump issued the 15 Days to Slow the Spread guidelines that governors used to close businesses by decree, then signed the $2.2 trillion CARES Act to pay people for a shutdown his own administration endorsed. A president who understood liberty would have defended every man's right to open his shop and earn his living. Why the pass?

You built a career attacking the welfare state. Trump Accounts hand $1,000 of taxpayer money to every child born from 2025 through 2028, the same baby bond scheme Democrats ran in their own cities. Redistribution with a president's name on it is still redistribution. Why the silence?

You were right that the Iranian regime had to be ended, and I agreed with you. A just war still has to be fought to win. Eight months in, at least 18 Americans are dead and more than 750 wounded, the regime still rules Tehran, and Trump has claimed a regime change that did not happen. Then he cut Israel almost entirely out of the talks, and Israeli officials warned that left Iran's ballistic missiles off the table. He stopped Netanyahu from hitting Iran's energy sites, reportedly told him to stop blowing up buildings, and called him a very difficult guy. In June he signed a memorandum offering sanctions waivers and a path to Tehran's frozen money, the same concession he spent years calling the fatal flaw of the JCPOA, in a deal that even reached into Israel's war in Lebanon. It expired without a deal and the fighting resumed. You called that deal a disaster for Israel on your own show, and still the man who signed it stayed above criticism. Why does Trump get a pass from you?

Then Trump lifted sanctions on Putin's diesel a month before the election, weeks after signing the sanctions law named for Lindsey Graham, and thanked Putin for it. That revenue pays for Russia's war on Ukraine and helps Moscow keep feeding Iran the targeting intelligence and drone parts it uses against American troops. Mike Pence and a dozen senators from both parties objected. Where were you?

Tucker did not lose this election. Voters looked at tariff inflation, record debt, and a foreign policy that bombs one enemy, offers it money, sidelines our ally, then props up another enemy, and they voted it out. The anger in your replies is about the standards you wrote down and then dropped.

So who is the spiritual leader here, and who is the follower who refuses to question him? And who has betrayed their own stated principles?

"Where Do We Go From Here?" seems to be the big question. I have an answer.
The answer is the same as it ever was.
We Keep Going Forwards Towards Enlightened Nationalism.
 
"Enlightened Nationalism" perfectly captures the pragmatic, high-minded realism that guided the early United States. 
There's no question our Founding Fathers were brilliant—enlightened nationalism was not some accidental byproduct of their actions; it was the deliberate, intellectual blueprint for the United States.

Enlightened nationalism puts the nation-state first in political accountability, cultural continuity, and economic strategy while preserving Enlightenment Principles: Individual Liberty, Reason, Evidence, Limited Government, and Merit.

It is neither ethnic nationalism nor borderless globalism. American Identity Is Civic, NOT Racial—rooted in the Constitution, rule of law, free speech, property rights, equal protection, and shared civic responsibility. Newcomers are Welcome, but Assimilation into that common framework Matters.

# Why it makes sense #

High-trust societies depend on shared language, norms, institutions, and civic expectations. Research on social capital, including Robert Putnam's work, raises legitimate questions about the effects of rapid, unassimilated diversity on social trust and civic cooperation.

Globalism has also exposed serious weaknesses:
- Strategic dependence on foreign supply chains, energy(oil) and competitors like China.
- Technology and intellectual-property transfers that undermine American industry.
- Immigration and asylum systems that can exceed fiscal, institutional, and assimilation capacity.
- Reduced democratic control over borders, trade, and national policy.

Isolationism sacrifices talent, markets, and strategic alliances.
*Multiculturalism Without Shared Civic Expectations Risks Replacing National Cohesion With Competing Identities.
*Supranational Institutions Cannot Replace Accountability to American Voters.

*What Enlightened Nationalism Means*

- **Civic, not racial:**
Citizenship is open to those who embrace America's constitutional framework, language, laws, and civic responsibilities.
- **Evidence over ideology:** Immigration policy should consider skills, fiscal impact, security, institutional capacity, and measurable assimilation outcomes.
- **Economic sovereignty:**
Reciprocal trade, domestic manufacturing, energy abundance, and strategic independence in semiconductors, pharmaceuticals, AI, and critical minerals.
- **Limited government:**
Secure borders, public order, competent education, constitutional protections, and institutions accountable to citizens—not transnational interests.
- **National interest first:**
Strong alliances, credible deterrence, and selective engagement without endless nation-building or unconditional global commitments.

→ The Practical Direction → 

Secure borders.
Enforce immigration law.
Prioritize merit and assimilation in legal immigration.
Restore domestic manufacturing and energy abundance.
Teach American history, constitutional principles, and academic competence. Protect free speech and equal treatment under the law.

Florida offers examples of state-level approaches emphasizing educational standards, energy development, and resistance to federal overreach.

The enduring principle is simple: Enlightened nationalism isn't about rejecting the world. It's about recognizing that America's first responsibility is to its own citizens.

National sovereignty, individual liberty, economic strength, cultural confidence, and constitutional government aren't competing ideals. They're the pillars of a Strong and Enduring American Republic.

text:
Stormy Daniels is still bitter about the dinner she never got. In 2006 Trump's bodyguard invited her to dinner, and she went up to his suite in Lake Tahoe. She was 27 and he was 60, and Melania had given birth to Barron a few months before. She stayed about three hours. No food ever came, they drank only water, and she doesn't think he drinks at all.

The suite was bigger than her first three apartments put together and had a conference table, a living room and a kitchen. He opened the door in silk pajamas. They talked business, she told him about her family and her dream of directing, and he pitched her on getting onto his TV show. At some point she kept calling her friend Alana Evans to come up, and according to Evans, Trump took the phone himself and invited her to party. When Stormy needed the bathroom he sent her through the bedroom, and she went through his toiletry bag. To this day she can name his shampoo and the pocket where he kept his gold-plated tweezers. In court she said it was Old Spice and Pert Plus.

She came out to find him perched on the bed in boxers and a T-shirt, doing what she calls the most tragic Burt Reynolds impression. Her heart dropped so hard she says it felt like it fell out of her vagina. When she tried to sidestep him, he got up and blocked the way, and his bodyguard was standing right outside the door. Then she blacked out. She insists there were no drugs and no alcohol. Her next memory is lying naked on the bed with him on top of her, no condom, on the opposite side of the bed from where they'd been standing, with no idea how her gold strappy heels came off. She never said no, she says, and she never said yes either. Afterward her hands shook so hard she could barely get the heels back on, and he called her honeybunch and said they should do it again. Evans says Stormy later told her Trump had chased her around the room in his tighty-whities.

They did meet again. A year later, in his bungalow at the Beverly Hills Hotel, she says he made her watch Shark Week with him.

Part of this never made it into her book, because she didn't remember it until she saw Bombshell in 2019. It came back to her in the theater, and she broke down in front of her date. What she remembers now is him telling her, right before, that if she didn't want to go back to Louisiana and wanted to be taken seriously as a director, she had to prove she'd do whatever it takes. On the stand she put it as him saying this was her only way out of the trailer park. Eric Trump sat behind his father in court while she told it.

The host pointed out that most porn girls escort, so a porn star going to a man's hotel room looks like a transaction. She said she wasn't escorting, that he never offered money and never paid her, and that all her friends are escorts and she's fine with it. If he had paid, she says, there'd be no story, because you don't sell out a client. These days she reads tarot cards for clients.

In 2018 she told Vogue it was normal-people sex and lasted maybe two minutes, and she was being generous. By 2024 she was testifying about an imbalance of power and a blackout, and Trump's lawyers asked for a mistrial over the details. The judge refused. Trump denies they ever had sex. Days before the 2016 election his lawyer paid her $130,000 to keep quiet, and in 2024 a jury convicted Trump on all 34 counts of hiding that payment.

She went upstairs for a dinner that never came, and a year later she was watching Shark Week with him. Did Trump con her with a TV show, or has Stormy kept changing her story about that night?

text:
Newt Lee Almost Framed: The Negro Night Watchman Who Discovered Mary Phagan's Body

As the story later developed in this series, he was almost framed by his boss: 

His Life, the Coroner's Inquest of April 30, 1913, the Leo Frank Murder Trial, and His Later Years

Principal newspaper: The Atlanta Constitution, Thursday, May 1, 1913, page 3.

Headline: “Newt Lee Tells His Story During Morning Session.”

On Wednesday, April 30, 1913, Newt Lee, the Negro night watchman at Atlanta's National Pencil Company, testified before Fulton County Coroner Paul V. Donehoo about discovering the body of 13-year-old Mary Anne Phagan. Lee had found her in the factory basement early Sunday morning, April 27, and had telephoned the police.

By the time he testified, Lee had spent three days in police custody. Detectives had questioned him repeatedly, examined his movements, and searched his home. Investigators found incriminating evidence, a blood soaked shirt, inside Lee's room, which was determined at first glance to be curiously contrived.

The following morning, The Atlanta Constitution, Thursday, May 1, 1913, page 3, reported that Lee had remained firm during questioning. The newspaper declared, “The most severe cross examination could not shake the negro” (AC, 3).

Lee's testimony described the events of Saturday, April 26, the discovery of Mary's body, and several actions by factory superintendent Leo M. Frank that Lee considered unusual. His account became an important part of the state's case against Frank.

Newt Lee's Birth, Family, and Employment

Newt Lee is believed to have been born around 1860, making him approximately 53 years old when Mary Phagan was murdered in 1913.

His exact birth date and early family history remain uncertain. Contemporary newspapers frequently called him Old Newt, but provided little information about his childhood, parents, or education.

In April 1913, Lee lived in Atlanta, boarding at the rear of 40 Henry Street.

Before working at the downtown National Pencil Company factory, he had been employed for several months as a night watchman at the company's Oakland plant. By April 26, he had worked at the South Forsyth Street factory for approximately three weeks.

Lee's duties included guarding the building, inspecting doors and windows, looking for signs of fire, and punching a mechanical time clock every thirty minutes. 

Frank had personally shown him how to make his rounds about the building when he began working there.

His regular hours began at 6:00 p.m. on weekdays and 5:00 p.m. on Saturdays. He worked until 6:30 a.m. when the day watchman would take over the security guard shift for the work day.

Saturday, April 26: Frank Sends Lee Away

On Friday, April 25, Frank told Lee to report at 4:00 p.m.  the following day, an hour earlier than usual because of the Confederate Memorial Day holiday. Frank had planned to go see the ball game with his Christian brother-in-law Mr. Ursenbach who was married to Lucille Selig Frank's older sister Rosalind Selig Ursenbach.

Lee arrived shortly before four and found the inner stairway doors locked. He considered this unusual because they had ordinarily been open.

He unlocked the doors, went upstairs, and announced his arrival.

According to Lee, Frank emerged from his office frenetically, rubbing his hands. Lee had never seen him behave that way before. It was strange behavior for Frank, especially on a quiet afternoon when the factory was shuttered. 

Frank apologized for having him report early and assertively told him to leave and return at six. Lee protested and asked if he could sleep on a cot in the packing room, but Frank refused. The factory superintendent Frank was likely hoping Conley would return that is if the janitor's story was to be believed about what happened earlier in the day. 

The Constitution reported Frank's instruction, as recalled by Lee: “Go out and have some more fun” (AC, 3).

Lee preferred to rest in the factory's shipping room, but Frank insisted that he leave. But why? Why must he leave the factory? Jim Conley's story gives us some clues.

Lee walked toward Decatur Street, where he watched an outdoor medicine show. He returned to the factory shortly before six.

When Lee returned, Frank changed the time-clock slip. Lee later testified that Frank appeared to have difficulty inserting it and took longer than usual. Frank was nervous putting in Lee's time slip into the clock. Was this a foreshadowing of what was to come with regard to the time slip?

The Visit of J. M. Gantt

Shortly after Lee returned, J. M. Gantt, a former National Pencil Company employee, appeared at the factory.

Gantt wanted to collect two pairs of shoes he had left in the building.

Lee initially refused to admit him without permission because Gantt had recently been discharged.

When Frank learned that Gantt was there, Lee said the superintendent appeared frightened.

Frank eventually allowed Gantt to retrieve his shoes, instructing Lee to accompany him.

Gantt collected the shoes and departed.

Lee also testified that Frank later left the factory. He could not establish whether the superintendent returned because Frank possessed a key.

Frank's Telephone Call

During his rounds that evening, Lee noticed that a basement gaslight had been turned down considerably.

He described the flame as being about as bright as a lightning bug.

Later, Frank telephoned the factory and asked whether everything was all right.

Lee considered the call unusual because Frank had never previously telephoned him during his night watch.

Lee answered that everything was satisfactory, and the conversation ended.

He continued his patrols, maintaining that he punched the time clock every thirty minutes throughout the night (BOE Lee, 3).

Sunday, April 27: The Discovery of Mary Phagan's Body

Shortly after 3:00 a.m., Lee descended into the basement to use the toilet. Afterward, he walked toward the rear of the building to inspect the area for fire and check the rear entrance.

He noticed something lying near an open partition.

At first, he thought someone had placed an object there to frighten him. When he approached, he realized that it was a human body.

Lee returned upstairs and telephoned police headquarters.

Officers arrived shortly afterward, and Lee led them into the basement.

There they found Mary Phagan's body, with a cord and cloth around her neck. Two handwritten notes were also discovered nearby.

Lee was arrested during the early investigation.

Wednesday, April 30: Lee Testifies at the Coroner's Inquest

The coroner's inquest resumed Wednesday morning at Atlanta Police Headquarters.

Coroner Donehoo presided over the proceedings, which began around 9:00 a.m.

Police officers testified about the condition of Mary's body, the basement lighting, and their interactions with Lee.

Lee took the witness stand at 11:45 a.m.

The Atlanta Constitution reported that his account remained steady under questioning, although several details were disputed.

The Position of Mary's Body

Lee insisted that Mary was lying on her back when he first saw her.

The responding officers testified that they found her face down, with her head toward the front of the building.

Lee denied touching or moving the body.

This disagreement troubled investigators because the two descriptions could not both be correct unless the body had been moved or someone had mistaken its position.

The Constitution suggested that the murderer might still have been concealed in the basement when Lee discovered the body. That explanation was newspaper speculation. No witness reported seeing another person move the body. 

Lee continued to insist that his recollection was accurate (AC, 3).

The Lantern and Identification of the Victim

Investigators also questioned how Lee could identify the victim in the darkness.

The responding officers described his lantern as dirty and dim.

Patrolman W. F. Anderson estimated that its light would permit visibility over only 12 to 15 feet. But the body was nearly 25 feet away or so. 

Lee said he had approached close enough to observe the girl's hair and exposed skin.

He denied examining or touching the body.

The disagreement concerned how clearly Lee could see and whether his account matched the physical conditions in the basement (AC, 3).

Sergeant Levi S. Dobbs and the Murder Notes

Sergeant Levi S. Dobbs testified about the two handwritten notes found near Mary's body.

One note referred to a Black night watchman and appeared to direct suspicion toward Lee.

Dobbs said he confronted Lee about the notes. Lee denied involvement.

Factory sweeper Jim Conley later admitted writing the notes and testified that Frank had directed him to do so to frame Newt Lee. Frank denied that accusation.

The notes became part of the prosecution's claim that someone had attempted to place responsibility for the murder on Lee.

The Disputed Time-Clock Slip

The watchman's time-clock record became one of the most contested pieces of evidence.

Lee maintained that he had made all his required punches throughout Saturday night.

On Sunday morning, Frank opened the clock in the presence of Lee, police officers, and factory foreman N. V. Darley. Frank said the slip was alright when he examined it.

Lee testified that Frank said the punches were correct and that he had not missed any (BOE Lee, 4).

W. W. Rogers, known as Boots Rogers, independently examined the slip. 

He testified:

“I glanced all the way down and there was a punch for every number” (BOE Rogers, 1).

Frank then took the slip back toward his office and it would remain in his custody.

Detective John R. Black testified that on Monday and Tuesday, Frank began saying that the clock had been mispunched three times. An examination of the slip indicated it had four individual hour time gaps spread out. How did it go from being punched correctly to have 4 half hour gaps

Other descriptions of the disputed intervals refer to four missing half-hour entries which created four total gaps of one hour. The difference between three irregular intervals and four expected punches requires examination of the actual clock slip.

The gaps mattered because they could suggest that Lee had enough time to leave the factory, go home, change his clothing, and return. It also meant he could potentially discard other incriminating evidence as well. 

The prosecution argued that the change in the record was part of an attempt to direct suspicion toward Lee.

Frank denied altering the slip. Although the witness accounts raised serious questions about its handling, they did not conclusively establish who changed any entries (BOE Rogers, 1; BOE Black, 2). The bottom line is that the time slip was in Frank's custody the entire time from when it was declared alright on Sunday and then suspicious on Monday. 

The Bloody Shirt Found at Lee's Home

On Tuesday, April 29, Detective John R. Black searched Lee's residence and found a bloodstained shirt in the bottom of a clothes barrel.

At first, the shirt appeared to support the theory that Lee might have left the factory, changed clothing, and hidden evidence. It meant that Lee was the killer if the shirt was accepted as anything other than forged and staged.

The prosecution later argued that the shirt had been planted. And a deeper analysis of the evidence suggests Bnai Brith executive and Leo Frank's attorney Herbert Haas may have orchestrated something. Haas demanded police search Leo Frank's dirty laundry, some two days after the murder, knowing they wouldn't find anything, but the intimation would send the police to investigate Newt Lee's room in a boarding house. 

During the trial, Solicitor General Hugh M. Dorsey accused Frank of attempting to direct suspicion toward Lee.

The bloody shirt, the disputed time-clock record, and the handwritten murder notes were presented as possible parts of the same effort.

In his closing argument, prosecutor Frank A. Hooper displayed the time slip and discussed the condition of the shirt.

He told the jury:

“It had to be planted. Gentlemen, it was planted!” (AC, 2).

Hooper then declared:

“He would sacrifice Newt Lee that he might live!” (AC, 2).

Lee was intended to be the Negro scapegoat for Leo Frank. The Negro would have hanged, and Leo Frank would have gone on with his life as if nothing happened.

These were the prosecution's arguments. They show that the possibility of a deliberate frame-up was raised during the original 1913 trial.

The testimony established that the shirt was found at Lee's residence and that the clock record was disputed only after Leo Frank pointed it out on Monday after saying on Sunday it was alright. It did not establish beyond dispute who planted the garment or whether Frank personally altered the time slip, but circumstantial evidence suggests it was likely a Bnai Brith plot. 

May 8: Lee Testifies Again

Lee returned to the coroner's inquest on Thursday, May 8.

He testified about a private conversation he had with Frank while both men were detained at police headquarters.

Lee said Frank questioned whether he knew something about the murder. Lee denied having any knowledge beyond discovering the body.

Frank disputed the account and said detectives had encouraged their meeting.

The coroner's jury recommended that both men be held for further investigation.

On May 23, the Fulton County grand jury indicted Frank for murder. Lee was not indicted.

July 1913: Lee Remains in Jail

Although Lee had not been indicted, authorities continued holding him as a material witness.

His attorneys sought his release through habeas corpus proceedings.

At a hearing on Saturday, July 12, Solicitor Dorsey acknowledged that he did not believe the evidence supported an indictment against Lee.

Judge W. D. Ellis nevertheless ordered him to remain in custody until Frank's trial.

The Atlanta Constitution, Sunday, July 13, reported the decision under the headline “Lee Must Remain Behind the Bars” (AC, July 13).

Lee had already spent more than two months in jail.

July 28 and 29: Lee Testifies at Frank's Trial

Frank's murder trial began Monday, July 28, 1913, before Judge Leonard Strickland Roan.

Lee was the prosecution's third witness.

Dorsey questioned him about his employment, Frank's instructions, Gantt's visit, the telephone call, the time clock, and the discovery of Mary's body.

Defense attorney Luther Z. Rosser then cross-examined him at length.

Rosser challenged differences between Lee's April 30 inquest statements and his trial testimony. He also questioned Lee's ability to see in the basement and whether someone could enter the factory without Frank knowing.

Lee maintained that his account was accurate.

The Atlanta Georgian, Tuesday, July 29, reported that Lee spent approximately four hours and forty minutes under examination and cross-examination. The newspaper described the essential points of his account as remaining unchanged, although it acknowledged discrepancies between the two proceedings (AG, July 29).

Lee also described the conditions of his detention.

During his trial testimony, he said detectives repeatedly awakened him for questioning and that he had received little sleep during the first days after his arrest.

These statements help explain the pressure he faced before appearing at the coroner's inquest (BOE Lee, 7).

August 26, 1913: Lee Is Released

On Monday, August 25, the jury convicted Leo Frank of Mary Phagan's murder.

The following morning, Dorsey petitioned Judge Roan for Lee's release.

Dorsey stated that investigators had conducted a thorough investigation and had found no evidence connecting Lee with the murder.

At 11:10 a.m. on Tuesday, August 26, 1913, Lee walked out of the Fulton County Tower after approximately 121 days in police custody.

The Atlanta Journal, August 26, page 3, reported his release under the headline “Newt Lee Leaves Tower, Starts Search for Job.”

Lee carried two baskets containing clothing and other belongings. He went to police headquarters to collect property taken when he was arrested.

He told reporters that he was uncertain about his home and marriage and intended to seek employment immediately (AJ, 3).

September 16, 1913: The Grand Jury Clears Lee

On Tuesday, September 16, 1913, the Fulton County grand jury formally returned a no-bill against Newt Lee.

This meant the grand jury declined to indict him for Mary Phagan's murder.

The Atlanta Constitution, Wednesday, September 17, 1913, page 3, column 3, reported the decision under the headline “No Bill Is Found Against Newt Lee.”

The newspaper stated that the grand jury's action eliminated Lee from the matter of criminal responsibility for the murder (AC, 3).

This was the formal end of Lee's position as a murder suspect in the Fulton County proceedings.

Newt Lee in the 1920 Census

The 1920 United States Census provides a possible clue to Lee's later life.

The census sheet supplied for this research was recorded in Atlanta, Fulton County, Georgia, on January 8, 1920. It is from Enumeration District 43, Sheet 6B.

Line 60 lists Newt Lee, a Black man aged 60, born in Georgia. His occupation appears as a laborer working in a laundry.

Line 61 lists Elizabeth Lee, a Black girl aged 12, also born in Georgia.

Both are recorded as boarders in a household headed by Bertha Johnson.

The census therefore supports a possible birth year of 1859 or 1860 for Newt and 1907 or 1908 for Elizabeth.

The shared surname and adjoining entries suggest a possible family relationship. However, because Elizabeth is listed as a boarder rather than explicitly as Newt's daughter, their relationship remains unproved.

If this is the same Newt Lee who testified in 1913, the record would show that he survived at least until January 1920 and was then employed as a laundry laborer.

There is also an unverified lead that Elizabeth lived into the 1980s. Her death record and her relationship to Newt need further checking.

The census offers a useful starting point for tracing the night watchman's life after the trial, but it cannot yet be treated as a confirmed identification.

SUMMARY: Newt Lee's Place in the Mary Phagan Case

Newt Lee worked at the downtown pencil factory for only three weeks before discovering Mary Phagan's body.

He reported the discovery to police, was arrested, testified twice at the coroner's inquest, and became an important witness at Frank's murder trial.

The prosecution argued that the murder notes, the disputed time-clock slip, and the bloodstained shirt found at Lee's residence were connected to an effort to place the blame on him.

Those accusations were raised during the original trial, although the exact circumstances surrounding the alteration of the time record and the placement of the shirt remained disputed.

Lee was held for 4 months without being indicted. He was released on August 26, 1913, and formally cleared by a grand-jury no-bill on September 16.

The 1920 census may provide information about his later employment and family, but further records are needed to confirm the identification.

His precise death date and final residence remain unknown.

References
